  ρ : ℝ := Classical.choose (Real.exists_eq_iff_sqrt_eq.mpr ⟨by norm_num, by ring⟩) -- real root of ρ² + ρ³ = 1
  μ₂ : ℝ := sInf {r | ∀ (seq : InfiniteCutSequence),
    supr (portion_ratio seq) ≤ r}
directions.proof_strategy: The upper bound μ₂ ≤ 1+ρ follows from the paper's construction and Proposition 1 on cyclic factor avoidance. The lower bound μ₂ ≥ 1+ρ requires showing that no infinite sequence of cuts can achieve a ratio strictly less than 1+ρ. This likely requires analyzing the combinatorial constraints on infinite words over the alphabet {0,1,2,3} with ratios 1:ρ:ρ²:ρ³, proving that any such word avoiding equal adjacent letters must contain a portion with ratio at least (1+ρ)/(ρ²+ρ³) = 1+ρ. A potential approach uses the substitution system properties: the map sending 0↦23 (or 32), 1↦0, 2↦1, 3↦2 shows that any valid infinite sequence must eventually approximate the fixed point, forcing portions near the extremal ratio.
directions.title: Optimality of the cake-cutting constant μ₂

directions.description: For a complete multipartite graph G = K_{n_1,...,n_m} with n_1 ≤ ... ≤ n_m, the path-free complex PF_t(G) is vertex decomposable if and only if t ≥ 2n_{m-1} - 1. Equivalently, this is exactly the range where PF_t(G) is shellable and sequentially Cohen-Macaulay. For t ≤ 2n_{m-1} - 2, the complex fails to be sequentially Cohen-Macaulay.

    (G : SimpleGraph (Σ i : Fin m, Fin (ns i)))
    (hG : IsCompleteMultipartite G) (t : ℕ) :
    VertexDecomposable (pathFreeComplex t G) ↔ t ≥ 2 * ns (Fin.last m - 1) - 1 := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Formalize simplicial complexes and vertex decomposability in Lean, then define PF_t(G) as the simplicial complex of vertex subsets with no induced P_t. Define complete multipartite graphs and their part-size ordering. The forward direction (t ≥ 2n_{m-1}-1 ⟹ vertex decomposable) requires formalizing the explicit structural decomposition of PF_t(G) as a union of join complexes with a size-truncation term, then proving each join component is vertex decomposable and that the union preserves this property. The reverse direction (t ≤ 2n_{m-1}-2 ⟹ not sequentially Cohen-Macaulay) requires constructing a specific non-Cohen-Macaulay witness face or showing the homology fails the sequential Cohen-Macaulay condition, potentially via a Mayer-Vietoris spectral sequence argument.
directions.title: Vertex decomposability threshold for path-free complexes of complete multipartite graphs

directions.description: The number of length-n quasinecklaces Q_k(n) is exactly k times the number of length-n necklaces N_k(n) for all k ≥ 2 and n ≥ 1.
directions.proof_strategy: Demonstrate that each necklace corresponds to exactly k quasinecklaces via rotational symmetry or quasinecklace construction rules.
directions.title: Proportionality of quasinecklaces to necklaces

directions.description: For every doubly regular tournament T on n vertices (where n ≡ 3 mod 4, n ≥ 3), the metric dimension β(T) ≤ 2⌈log₂ n⌉. This extends the paper's O(log n) bound proven for certain doubly regular team tournaments to the classical and well-studied family of doubly regular tournaments, which are regular tournaments with parameters (n, (n-1)/2, (n-3)/4). The conjecture posits an explicit constant of 2, making it directly falsifiable by computing metric dimensions of small doubly regular tournaments (n = 3, 7, 11, 19, ...) and checking against the bound.

  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Adapt Babai's probabilistic method as used in the paper: for a doubly regular tournament T, randomly sample k = 2⌈log₂ n⌉ vertices as a resolving set candidate. Compute the probability that two distinct vertices u, v receive the same distance vector from the sampled set. Use the strong regularity properties of doubly regular tournaments—specifically that every pair of vertices has exactly (n-3)/4 common out-neighbours—to bound the collision probability per pair by 1/2^k. Apply a union bound over all n(n-1)/2 pairs, choosing k so that the union bound is < 1, yielding a resolving set of size at most 2⌈log₂ n⌉.
directions.title: Logarithmic metric dimension of doubly regular tournaments

directions.description: The paper proves that for $k \ge 3$ and sufficiently large $n$, the maximum size of a subset of the $n \times n$ grid with no $k+1$ collinear points is exactly $kn$. This conjecture posits that the condition 'sufficiently large $n$' can be relaxed to $n > k$, meaning $f_k(n) = kn$ holds for all $k \ge 3$ and $n > k$. This would unify the trivial case ($n \le k$, where $f_k(n) = n^2$) and the asymptotic regime.

    ∃ S : Finset (ℤ × ℤ), 
      S ⊆ Finset.product (Finset.range n) (Finset.range n) ∧
      S.card = k * n ∧
      (∀ (a b c : ℤ), (a ≠ 0 ∨ b ≠ 0) → 
        (Finset.filter (fun p : ℤ × ℤ => a * p.1 + b * p.2 + c = 0) S).card ≤ k) :=
  by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Either refine the probabilistic and pseudorandom hypergraph matching arguments to explicitly compute the threshold $N(k)$ and show it is $k+1$, or find a constructive algebraic or combinatorial proof that works uniformly for all $n > k$.
directions.title: Exact Threshold for No-$(k+1)$-in-line Problem

directions.description: For all natural numbers m, a, and d, the sum over all m-tuples (i_1, ..., i_m) of non-negative integers summing to d of the product of binomial coefficients ∏_{j=1}^{m} C(a + i_j, a) equals C(ma + d + m - 1, d). This generalizes the identity stated in the paper for m=3 (used to simplify the Bogart-Longyear formula for 3-row Latin rectangles), where the paper claims it is 'easily proved with dots and dividers.' The generalization connects directly to Gessel's framework through multisymmetric function generating series.

  ∑ t in Finset.Nat.antidiagonalTuple m d, 
    ∏ j : Fin m, (Nat.choose (a + t j) a) = 
  Nat.choose (m * a + d + m - 1) d := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Use generating functions: (1) establish that the ordinary generating function for C(a+i, a) is (1-x)^{-(a+1)} via the negative binomial theorem; (2) the product of m copies gives (1-x)^{-m(a+1)}, so the LHS is the coefficient of x^d; (3) extract the coefficient as C(m(a+1)+d-1, d) = C(ma+d+m-1, d). Alternatively, prove by induction on m using Vandermonde convolution as the inductive step, with the m=1 base case being trivial.
directions.title: Generalized Multinomial Convolution Identity for Latin Rectangle Enumeration

directions.description: There are mathematical objects whose existence we can prove but whose specific properties are unknowable — theorems that cast shadows without being visible. Define a dark theorem as a statement T such that: (1) PA proves 'there exists x such that T(x)', but (2) for every specific n, PA does NOT prove T(n). The classic example is the Paris-Harrington theorem: the strengthened finite Ramsey theorem is true but not provable in PA. But dark theorems go further: they assert the existence of objects that no specific instance can be verified. Conjecture: The set of dark theorems is dense in the space of all Pi_2 statements — most true Pi_2 statements are dark. Moreover, there is a hierarchy of darkness: a dark theorem of level k is one where PA proves 'there exist at least k values of x such that T(x)' but cannot identify any specific one. The hierarchy is strict: level k+1 dark theorems are strictly harder to prove than level k. Test: construct explicit dark theorems of levels 1, 2, 3 using the Paris-Harrington principle and the Kirby-Paris hydra theorem. Prove the density conjecture by counting Pi_2 statements. Impact: most true mathematical statements are dark — they assert existence without the possibility of verification. This is not incompleteness; it is a new form of mathematical unknowability.
directions.proof_strategy: Define a dark theorem of level k as a Pi_2 statement 'for all n, there exist at least k values of m such that P(n,m)' such that PA proves the existential claim but PA does not prove P(n,m) for any specific m. Level 1: Paris-Harrington theorem (the strengthened finite Ramsey theorem). Level 2: the Paris-Harrington theorem for the statement 'there exist at least 2 values of m satisfying the Ramsey property'. Prove strictness: if T is level k+1, then T implies a level-k statement that is independent of PA. Prove density: among all Pi_2 statements provable in ZFC, the fraction that are dark approaches 1 as statement length grows. Test: formalize levels 1-3 in Lean 4 using the Paris-Harrington and Goodstein sequences.
directions.title: Dark Mathematics: Theorems That Exist But Cannot Be Found

directions.description: The brain's connectome is a braid: neurons fire in sequences that interleave like strands of a braid group. Formalize this: a cognitive process is an element of the braid group B_n where n is the number of brain regions. Two cognitive processes are equivalent if their braids are related by Reidemeister moves (cognitive equivalence). Conjecture: The Jones polynomial of a cognitive braid is invariant under cognitive equivalence and encodes the information content of the thought. A thought with Jones polynomial V(t) = 1 is a trivial thought (equivalent to no thinking). A thought with V(t) = -t^2 + t + 1 is a creative thought (it contains a trefoil knot — the simplest non-trivial braid). The information content of a thought is log(|V(e^{2pi i/3})|), which measures the quantum dimension of the braid. Test: compute the Jones polynomial of braids representing simple cognitive processes (linear reasoning: trivial braid, creative insight: trefoil, confused thinking: figure-eight knot) and verify that the quantum dimension correlates with subjective ratings of thought quality. Impact: thinking IS braiding. The topology of your thoughts determines their quality. Creative insights are literally knotted.
directions.proof_strategy: Define cognitive braids: each brain region is a strand, each neural firing sequence is a crossing. A cognitive process is an element of B_n (braid group on n strands). Two thoughts are equivalent if related by Reidemeister moves. Define thought quality Q(braid) = log(|V_braid(e^{2pi i/3})|) where V is the Jones polynomial. Prove Q is a braid invariant. Prove: trivial braid has V = 1 so Q = 0 (trivial thought). Trefoil has V = -t^2+t+1 so Q = log(|V(e^{2pi i/3})|) = log(sqrt(3)) > 0 (creative thought). Figure-eight has Q = log(2) (confused thought with maximum entanglement). Test: compute Jones polynomials for braids B_3 representing simple cognitive processes and rank by Q.
directions.title: Knots That Think: Cognition as Braiding in Category Theory

directions.description: Mendeleev organized 63 elements into a periodic table that predicted undiscovered elements. Can we do the same for finite groups? Classify all finite groups of order <= 2000 (there are approximately 10^15 of them, so we need a structural organization). Define group families as 'chemical series': cyclic groups are noble gases (stable, simple structure), symmetric groups are halogens (highly reactive, generate all finite groups), simple groups are transition metals (rare, catalytic). Conjecture: The 'periodic law' for finite groups is: groups in the same column (same family type) have isomorphic composition factors. The 'atomic number' is the order, and the 'valence' is the number of minimal normal subgroups. Groups with the same composition factors but different orders are 'isotopes' — they share chemical properties (solubility = solvability, reactivity = generation capacity). Test: construct a periodic table of groups of order <= 100, organizing them by composition factors. Verify that groups in the same column share key properties (nilpotency class, derived length, automorphism group order). Predict the properties of undiscovered groups (e.g., order 120, composition factors {2,2,2,3,5}) before looking them up. Impact: a chemical-mathematical analogy that makes the classification of finite groups intuitive and predictive.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the periodic table of finite groups: rows indexed by order (atomic number), columns indexed by composition factor pattern (chemical series). Group types: cyclic (noble gases), symmetric (halogens), simple non-abelian (transition metals), nilpotent (alkali metals), solvable non-nilpotent (alkaline earth). Prove: groups in the same column have isomorphic composition factors (Jordan-Holder theorem). Prove: the 'valence' (number of minimal normal subgroups) is determined by the chief factors. Construct the table for order <= 100 and verify periodicity: cyclic groups of prime order form the first column, groups with composition {2,2,3} form the second column, etc. Test: predict properties of groups of order 120 before computing them.
directions.title: The Periodic Table of Finite Groups: Chemistry Meets Algebra

directions.description: The AdS/CFT correspondence says that a gravitational theory in the bulk of anti-de Sitter space is equivalent to a conformal field theory on the boundary. What if prime numbers have a holographic dual? Define the prime hologram: for each prime p, define its 'boundary' as the ring Z/pZ and its 'bulk' as the p-adic field Q_p. Conjecture: The Riemann zeta function zeta(s) = prod_p (1 - p^{-s})^{-1} is the holographic partition function: the product over primes (boundary) encodes the same information as the completed zeta function Xi(s) (bulk). The functional equation Xi(s) = Xi(1-s) is the holographic duality: bulk physics at depth s equals boundary physics at depth 1-s. The prime counting function pi(x) ~ x/log(x) is the bulk volume, while the Chebyshev function theta(x) = sum_{p<=x} log(p) is the boundary area. The AdS/CFT dictionary: bulk gravity mode at depth s <-> boundary CFT operator of dimension 1-s. Test: verify that the pair correlation of zeta zeros matches GUE random matrices (bulk = quantum gravity in AdS, boundary = CFT random matrix ensemble). Compute the 'prime partition function' Z(beta) = prod_p (1 - e^{-beta log p})^{-1} and show it equals the bulk partition function. Impact: the Riemann Hypothesis is equivalent to a holographic stability condition — zeros on the critical line means the bulk geometry is stable against perturbations.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the prime partition function Z(beta) = prod_p (1 - e^{-beta log p})^{-1}. Prove Z(beta) = zeta(s) where beta = Re(s)/log(p) in the saddle-point approximation. Define the holographic dictionary: bulk field phi_s(x) in AdS_3 <-> boundary CFT operator O_{1-s}(y) on S^1. Prove the correspondence: phi_s <-> (1 - p^{-s})^{-1} for each prime p. The functional equation Xi(s) = Xi(1-s) is the holographic duality. Prove: if all zeros of Xi(s) are on Re(s) = 1/2, then the bulk AdS geometry is stable (no tachyonic modes). Conversely, an off-critical-line zero at s = 1/2 + epsilon corresponds to a tachyonic instability in the bulk. Test: compute Z(beta) numerically and verify convergence to zeta(s).
directions.title: Holographic Primes: The Prime Number AdS/CFT Correspondence

directions.description: Every real number defines a musical scale: map the digits 0-9 to frequencies f_n = 220 * 2^{n/12} (the A minor pentatonic scale extended). The number pi = 3.14159265... produces the sequence E4, C5, C#5, D5, D#5, F5, E5, A4, G5, C5... — a melody. Conjecture: The melody of pi is not periodic (because pi is irrational) but has musical structure: the autocorrelation of the digit sequence at lag 12 (one octave) is positive and statistically significant. This means pi has more octave-related notes than expected by chance — pi 'favors' notes separated by octaves. Similarly, e 'favors' perfect fifths (lag 7) and sqrt(2) 'favors' minor thirds (lag 3). The musical structure of transcendental numbers reflects their continued fraction properties: numbers with bounded partial quotients have more consonant melodies. Test: compute the digit autocorrelation of pi, e, and sqrt(2) at lags 0-12 (representing unison through octave). Perform a chi-squared test comparing to the uniform distribution. Generate the 'music' of each constant and analyze for tonal centers. Impact: transcendental numbers have musical souls — their digit sequences contain hidden harmonies that reflect their deepest arithmetic properties.
directions.proof_strategy: Map digits 0-9 to frequencies f_n = 220 * 2^{n/12} Hz (chromatic scale starting at A3). Define the melody M(x) for a real number x as the sequence of frequencies corresponding to its decimal digits. Compute the autocorrelation R(k) = sum_{i} (d_i - 4.5)(d_{i+k} - 4.5) / N for lags k = 0,1,...,12. Under the null hypothesis (digits are uniformly random), R(k) ~ Normal(0, 1/N). Test: compute R(k) for pi (first 10^6 digits), e (first 10^6 digits), sqrt(2) (first 10^6 digits). If R(k) > 2/sqrt(N) for some k, that lag is statistically significant. Verify: pi has R(12) > threshold (octave preference), e has R(7) > threshold (fifth preference), sqrt(2) has R(3) > threshold (minor third preference). Connect to continued fractions: bounded partial quotients imply more structure in digit autocorrelations.
directions.title: The Sound of Pi: Musical Structure in Transcendental Constants

directions.description:
# Future Directions: Log-Concavity in the d-Hoggatt Hierarchy

This cycle established a sharp dichotomy for the *total* d-Hoggatt numbers
`H_d(n) = ∑_k H_d(n,k)`: the `d = 1` totals `2^n` are infinitely log-concave
(indeed log-linear), while the `d = 2` totals (Catalan numbers) are strictly
log-convex, and the `d = 3` totals (Baxter numbers) are empirically log-convex.
The following conjectures are the natural next targets.

## Conjecture 1 — Universal log-convexity of the totals for d ≥ 2

For every `d ≥ 2`, the total d-Hoggatt numbers are strictly log-convex:
`H_d(n+1)² < H_d(n) · H_d(n+2)` for all `n ≥ 0`.

The key insight is that each `H_d(n)` is a positively weighted sum of products
of binomial coefficients whose dominant growth ratio increases with `n`, so the
totals inherit the log-convexity of the Catalan case rather than the
log-concavity of the individual rows. Why now? The Catalan (`d = 2`) case is now
settled from a two-term recurrence, and the Baxter (`d = 3`) case matches it
term-by-term in the computed data, suggesting a single recurrence-driven
argument covers the whole family.

## Conjecture 2 — Row-sum log-convexity is a summation phenomenon

If `T(n,k)` is any triangle whose rows are log-concave and whose row-ratio
`T(n+1,k)/T(n,k)` is nondecreasing in `n`, then the row sums `S(n) = ∑_k T(n,k)`
are log-convex.

The key insight is that log-convexity of the totals is not special to Hoggatt
triangles but follows from monotone amplification of a common growth factor
across rows, a Chebyshev-sum / rearrangement effect. Why now? Having seen the
same negative discriminant `Δ_n < 0` for both Catalan and Baxter totals, the
phenomenon is clearly structural rather than coincidental and deserves a triangle
-level hypothesis.

## Conjecture 3 — Infinite log-concavity of the rows

For every `d ≥ 1`, each fixed row `k ↦ H_d(n,k)` of the d-Hoggatt triangle is
infinitely log-concave.

The key insight is that the log-concavity operator, when applied to a finite
positive log-concave row with the golden-ratio-squared safety factor
`a_k² ≥ ((3+√5)/2) · a_{k-1} a_{k+1}`, reproduces that same safety factor, so a
single closure lemma propagates through all iterates. Why now? The threshold
constant `(3+√5)/2` is exactly the fixed point of the operator's worst-case
ratio, and the toolkit built this cycle (the operator `𝓛`, its annihilation of
log-linear sequences, and closure under products) already contains the moving
parts needed to attack the closure lemma.

## Conjecture 4 — A log-concave "renormalization" of the totals

For every `d ≥ 2` there is an explicit positive normalizing sequence `w_d(n)`
(e.g. a ratio of factorials) such that the renormalized totals
`H_d(n) / w_d(n)` are infinitely log-concave, even though the raw totals are
log-convex.

The key insight is that log-convexity of the totals is caused by a smooth,
predictable growth factor which can be divided out, leaving a residual sequence
governed by the same infinite-log-concavity mechanism as the rows. Why now? The
exact growth ratio `(n+2)(2n+3)/((2n+1)(n+3))` for the Catalan totals is now
known in closed form, giving a concrete first candidate for `w_2` and a template
for higher `d`.

## Conjecture 5 — Tropical dequantization of the dichotomy

Under the tropical (min-plus) limit that sends a positive sequence `a_n` to its
valuations `v_n = −log a_n`, log-concavity becomes convexity of `v` and
log-linearity becomes affinity of `v`. The `d = 1`/`d ≥ 2` dichotomy then reads:
`v` is affine for `d = 1` and strictly concave for `d ≥ 2`.

The key insight is that the log-concavity operator degenerates, in the tropical
limit, to a second finite difference, so infinite log-concavity corresponds to a
sequence of iterated finite differences retaining a fixed sign — a purely
piecewise-linear, tropical-geometric condition. Why now? Casting the numeric
dichotomy in the min-plus semiring links this combinatorial question to tropical
convexity, where second-difference sign conditions are the natural objects and
powerful piecewise-linear tools are available.
directions.title: Sharp dichotomy for the *total* d-Hoggatt numbers

directions.description: The constant μ₂ is defined as the infimum over all infinite sequences of radial cuts of a unit circular cake of the supremum over n of the ratio (maximum portion size)/(minimum portion size) after n cuts, where a portion is an adjacent pair of slices. The paper proves μ₂ ≤ 1 + ρ where ρ ≈ 0.75488 is the unique real root of ρ² + ρ³ = 1. The conjecture asserts this bound is tight: μ₂ = 1 + ρ, meaning no cutting strategy can achieve a worst-case portion ratio strictly below 1 + ρ. This would also establish μ₂ as irrational, since ρ is irrational.
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
import Mathlib.Data.Real.Basic
import Mathlib.Data.Real.Irrational

-- The unique real root of ρ² + ρ³ = 1 in (0,1)
noncomputable def rho : ℝ :=
  sorry -- defined as the unique real root

theorem rho_spec : rho ^ 2 + rho ^ 3 = 1 := sorry
theorem rho_pos : (0 : ℝ) < rho := sorry
theorem rho_lt_one : rho < (1 : ℝ) := sorry

-- A portion is a pair of adjacent slices; portion_ratio computes
-- max_portion / min_portion after n cuts for a given cut sequence
noncomputable def portion_ratio (cuts : ℕ → ℝ) (n : ℕ) : ℝ := sorry

-- μ₂ is the infimum over all infinite cut sequences of the
-- supremum over n of the portion ratio
noncomputable def mu₂ : ℝ :=
  sInf { r | ∃ cuts : ℕ → ℝ,
    ∀ n, portion_ratio cuts n ≤ r }

/-- The optimal worst-case portion ratio equals 1 + ρ.
    The upper bound follows from the constructive algorithm in the paper.
    The lower bound remains open. -/
theorem mu₂_eq_one_plus_rho : mu₂ = 1 + rho := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: The upper bound μ₂ ≤ 1 + ρ is proven constructively via a specific cutting algorithm and a word-avoidance argument over {0,1,2,3}. The lower bound μ₂ ≥ 1 + ρ remains wide open (only μ₂ ≥ 5/3 is known). A plausible approach: (1) Show that any infinite cutting sequence achieving ratio < 1 + ρ must, after sufficient normalization, produce slices whose sizes lie in ratios from {1, ρ, ρ², ρ³}, (2) Prove that the corresponding word over {0,1,2,3} must avoid all factors in the forbidden set A from Proposition O, (3) Show by combinatorial or automata-theoretic means that no infinite word cyclically avoiding A can have all adjacent-pair sums below 1 + ρ times the minimum adjacent-pair sum. Alternatively, a potential-function argument tracking the distribution of slice sizes could force a lower bound.
directions.title: The optimal portion ratio μ₂ equals 1 + ρ

directions.description: For a complete multipartite graph $K_{n_1, \dots, n_m}$ with $n_1 \le \dots \le n_m$ and $m \ge 2$, the $t$-path-free complex $\PF_t(K_{n_1, \dots, n_m})$ is vertex decomposable if and only if $t \ge 2n_{m-1} - 1$.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem pf_vertex_decomposable_iff {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] {m : ℕ} (ns : Fin m → ℕ) (h_sorted : Monotone ns) (h_m : 2 ≤ m) (t : ℕ) : VertexDecomposable (PF t (completeMultipartiteGraph ns)) ↔ 2 * ns ⟨m - 2, by omega⟩ ≤ t + 1 := by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: First formalize abstract simplicial complexes, the $t$-path-free complex $\PF_t(G)$, and vertex decomposability in Lean. Then, formalize the structural decomposition of $\PF_t(G)$ as a union of join complexes. Establish that for $t \le 2n_{m-1} - 2$, the complex fails to be sequentially Cohen-Macaulay by analyzing the link of a specific face. Finally, prove vertex decomposability for $t \ge 2n_{m-1} - 1$ by explicitly constructing the shedding vertex sequence and applying the decomposition theorem.
directions.title: Vertex Decomposability of Path-Free Complexes of Complete Multipartite Graphs

directions.description: For an elliptic curve E over Q with good supersingular reduction at 2 and square-free conductor N_E, and a square-free integer D > 0 congruent to 1 mod 4, the difference between the sharp/flat 2-adic Iwasawa lambda-invariants of the quadratic twist E^D and E (assuming the mu-invariant is 0) is given by the sum over prime divisors ell of D of 2^{n_ell} (if ell divides N_E) or 2^{n_ell+1} (if ell does not divide N_E and 2 divides the order of E modulo ell), where n_ell is the 2-adic valuation of (ell^2 - 1)/8.
directions.proof_strategy: Formalize quadratic twists of elliptic curves, the reduction of elliptic curves modulo primes, the order of the finite group of rational points, and the definition of Sprung's sharp/flat 2-adic L-functions. Then establish the explicit difference formula for the lambda-invariants by evaluating the sum over the prime divisors of D using the local properties of the 2-adic L-function under quadratic twists.
directions.title: Matsuno-type Formula for Supersingular Iwasawa Lambda-Invariants

directions.description: We conjecture that for every positive integer n, the signed adjacency matrix M_n of the dual graph of the triangular region T_n has eigenvalues exactly π_k = 2 cos(π k/(3n+3)) for k = 1,2,…,3n+2, excluding k = n+1 and k = 2n+2. Consequently, the determinant of M_n (which counts lozenge tilings) equals the product ∏_{k∈S_n} π_k, matching the product formula proved in the paper.
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
theorem eigenvalues_of_M_n (n : ℤ) :
  ∀ k : ℤ, k ≤ 3*n + 2 → k ≠ n + 1 → k ≠ 2*n + 2 →
    isEigenvalue (M_n n) (2 * Real.cos (Pi * ʹk / (3*n + 3))) := by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Apply discrete Fourier transform on the cyclic group ℤ_{3n+3} to diagonalize M_n. The eigenvectors are given by characters χ_j(v) = ζ^{jv} where ζ = e^{2πi/(3n+3)}. Computing M_n·χ_j yields eigenvalue π_j = ζ^a + ζ^b + ζ^{-a-b} for appropriate a,b, which simplifies to 2 cos(π j/(3n+3)). The exceptional pair (n+1,2n+2) corresponds to a zero eigenvalue, which is omitted from the spectrum. Hence the eigenvalues are exactly the claimed cosines, and the determinant matches the product formula.
directions.title: Eigenvalue conjecture for the signed adjacency matrix M_n of the triangular region's dual graph

directions.description: Mathematics is full of impossibility theorems — things that CANNOT be done. But impossibility theorems are themselves beautiful mathematical objects. Catalog and interconnect the great impossibilities: (1) Squaring the circle (pi is transcendental, Lindemann 1882). (2) Trisecting the angle (cos 20 degrees has degree 3 over Q, Wantzel 1837). (3) Doubling the cube (cube root of 2 has degree 3, Wantzel 1837). (4) Solving the quintic by radicals (A_5 is not solvable, Abel-Ruffini 1824). (5) The Borsuk-Ulam impossibility (every continuous map S^n -> R^n has a point where f(x) = f(-x)). (6) Arrow's impossibility (no voting system is simultaneously fair, complete, and non-dictatorial). (7) Heisenberg's uncertainty (Delta x * Delta p >= hbar/2). Conjecture: These impossibility theorems are connected by a deep structural principle — each one arises because a certain group action is not free. Squaring the circle fails because Gal(Q(pi)/Q) acts freely. Solving the quintic fails because A_5 acts freely on the roots. Arrow's theorem fails because the symmetric group acts freely on preferences. Heisenberg fails because the Heisenberg group acts freely on phase space. The unified principle: a task is impossible iff the relevant group action is free. Test: verify that each impossibility theorem corresponds to a free group action. Prove the converse: if a group G acts freely on a set X, then there exists a G-equivariant task that is impossible on X. Impact: all impossibility is the same impossibility — every CAN'T is a reflection of a free group action.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the impossibility correspondence: an impossibility theorem T corresponds to a group G acting freely on a set X. Squaring the circle: G = Gal(Q(pi)/Q) acts freely on Q(pi). Quintic: G = A_5 acts freely on the set of roots. Arrow: G = S_n acts freely on preference profiles. Heisenberg: G = Heisenberg group acts freely on phase space R^{2n}. Prove: if G acts freely on X, then no G-equivariant map X -> X/G exists that is a section of the quotient map (this is the impossibility). Prove the converse: if no such section exists, then some subgroup of G acts freely on X. The key lemma: a section of X -> X/G exists iff the action has a fixed point. Test: verify the correspondence for all seven impossibility theorems.
directions.title: Impossibility Results for Fun: Things That Cannot Be Done (But We Try Anyway)

directions.description: Conway's surreal numbers No form the largest totally ordered field, containing all real numbers, all ordinals, and all infinitesimals. But No is a proper class, not a set. What topology does it have? Conjecture: No has a unique topology making it a connected, locally connected, locally compact, complete ordered field. This topology is NOT the order topology (which makes No totally disconnected). Instead, it is the 'interval topology' generated by open intervals (a,b) = {x in No : a < x < b} where a,b are arbitrary surreal numbers. The interval topology on No is connected because between any two surreals a < b there are infinitely many surreals, and No has no gaps (every Dedekind cut is filled). Moreover, No is contractible in this topology — every surreal number can be continuously deformed to 0 via the homotopy H(x,t) = x * {t | 0} where {t | 0} is the surreal number between t and 0. Test: prove that No with the interval topology is connected. Prove that it is locally compact (every surreal has a neighborhood basis of intervals with surreal endpoints). Prove that No is contractible. Compute the fundamental group: pi_1(No) = 0 (trivial, since No is contractible). Impact: the largest ordered field has a natural topology that makes it contractible — every surreal number is connected to every other by a continuous path.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the interval topology on No: a basis of open sets is {(a,b) : a,b in No, a < b}. Prove No is connected: if No = U union V with U,V disjoint open, take a in U, b in V, a < b. Then (a,b) intersects both U and V, contradicting disjointness. Actually, No with interval topology IS disconnected (intervals with surreal endpoints can be partitioned). The correct topology: the 'convex topology' where open sets are unions of convex subsets. Prove No is connected in the convex topology because every interval {x : a < x < b} is connected (convex). Prove local compactness: every point has a neighborhood basis of intervals with finite-length endpoints. Prove contractibility: H(x,t) = x * t for t in [0,1] (using the Conway normal form). Compute pi_1(No) = 0. Test: verify the interval topology is strictly finer than the order topology for infinitesimal neighborhoods.
directions.title: Surreal Topology: What Topology Does the Field of Surreal Numbers Have?

directions.description: Bitcoin mining requires finding a nonce n such that SHA256(block_header || n) < target. What if we replaced SHA256 with a tropical hash? Define tropical SHA as: TSHA(m) = min over all i of (m_i + h_i) where m = (m_1,...,m_k) is the message, h = (h_1,...,h_k) is the tropical hash key, and all operations are in the min-plus semiring (a tropical plus b = min(a,b), a tropical times b = a + b). Conjecture: TSHA is a one-way function in the tropical sense: computing TSHA(m) given m and h is O(k) (trivial), but finding m given TSHA(m) and h is NP-hard (it reduces to a tropical shortest path problem). More precisely, the tropical preimage problem — given y and h, find m such that min_i(m_i + h_i) = y — requires checking O(e^{k}) tropical paths in the worst case. But there's a twist: tropical hash collisions are COMMON because min(a,b) = min(b,a). To fix this, define TSHA2(m) = (min_i(m_i + h_i), min_i(m_i + h'_i)) where h and h' are two independent tropical keys. Conjecture: TSHA2 is collision-resistant with probability 1 - O(1/k). Test: implement TSHA and TSHA2, measure collision resistance, and compare mining difficulty to SHA256 for block sizes k = 32, 64, 128. Impact: a cryptocurrency where mining is solving tropical optimization problems instead of brute-force hash searches — mining IS mathematics.
directions.proof_strategy: Define TSHA(m, h) = min_{i=1..k} (m_i + h_i) in the min-plus semiring. Prove: TSHA is O(k) to compute (single pass). Prove: finding m given TSHA(m,h) = y and h is NP-hard by reduction from the tropical shortest path problem. Reduction: given a weighted graph G, let h encode the edge weights and let m encode the path. Then TSHA(m,h) = length of shortest path. Finding m that achieves a given TSHA value equals finding the shortest path. Prove TSHA2 collision resistance: P(TSHA2(m) = TSHA2(m')) = O(1/k) for random h, h'. Test: implement TSHA, TSHA2, compare collision rates with SHA256 for k = 32, 64, 128. Measure mining time as function of difficulty.
directions.title: Tropical Cryptocurrency: Mining on the Min-Plus Semiring

directions.description: Suppose we had an oracle that computes L(s, chi) for any L-function and any complex s in O(1) time. What theorems would follow? Conjecture: The L-function oracle implies (1) The Riemann Hypothesis (compute zeros directly), (2) The BSD conjecture (compute the order of vanishing at s=1), (3) The Sato-Tate conjecture (compute the distribution of a_p), (4) Langlands functoriality (compare L-functions on both sides of the functoriality lift), and (5) A polynomial-time algorithm for factoring (the L-function of an elliptic curve E over Z/nZ detects factors of n). But the oracle also implies IMPOSSIBILITY results: (6) P != NP (because NP-complete problems would reduce to L-function computations that the oracle solves in O(1), contradicting the time hierarchy theorem if P = NP). Wait — the oracle solves L-function computations in O(1), so if P = NP, then NP problems can be encoded as L-function computations and solved instantly, but the oracle's existence is an axiom, not a theorem. The correct statement: the L-function oracle collapses the polynomial hierarchy to L-function computations. Test: prove that the Riemann Hypothesis follows from the oracle. Prove that BSD follows. Prove that factoring is in P given the oracle. Impact: understanding what an L-function oracle implies tells us exactly how powerful L-functions are — and how far we are from proving things about them.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the L-oracle O(s, chi) = L(s, chi) for any L-function chi and complex s. RH: compute all zeros of zeta(s) by evaluating zeta(s) on a fine grid and checking sign changes — O(R^2) oracle calls for zeros up to height R. BSD: compute L(E, 1) and check if it's zero (rank >= 1) or compute the Taylor expansion around s=1 to get the order of vanishing. Sato-Tate: compute a_p(E) for all p up to N by evaluating L(s, E) at s = it for varying t, and extract a_p from the Euler product. Factoring: given n = pq, define E: y^2 = x^3 + ax + b over Z/nZ. The oracle computes L(s, E/nZ), which has different values for different factorizations. Binary search on a to find p. P != NP: if the oracle exists as a physical device, then L-function computations are O(1), but the oracle itself cannot solve NP problems unless P = NP.
directions.title: The L-Function Oracle: What If We Could Compute L-Functions Instantly?

directions.description: The Moebius band M is obtained from [0,1] x R by identifying (0, y) ~ (1, -y). Define arithmetic on M: a point (x, y) on M represents the number y * (2x - 1) where x in [0,1] gives the sign and magnitude, and y gives the scale. This creates a number system where going around the band flips the sign. Define the Moebius integers Z_M as the image of Z in M under the embedding n -> (1/2 + 1/(2n), |n|). Then 1 and -1 are identified at the twist point (1, 1) = (0, -1), making Z_M a one-point compactification of Z with a single infinity. Conjecture: Z_M is a ring under the induced operations from R x R / ~, but it is NOT an integral domain because (1, 0) * (0, 1) = (0, 0) but neither factor is zero in Z_M. The prime factorization in Z_M has a unique 'twist prime' that encodes orientation, and every non-zero Moebius integer has a factorization of the form ±p_1^{a_1} * ... * p_k^{a_k} where the overall sign is the twist. Test: factor the Moebius integers 6, -6, and 0 in Z_M. Verify that 6 = 2_+ * 3_+ and -6 = 2_- * 3_- = 2_+ * 3_+ * (-1) where -1 is the twist prime. Impact: arithmetic on a non-orientable surface creates a number system where orientation IS a prime — a number-theoretic analog of spin in physics.
directions.proof_strategy: Define Z_M as the image of Z in the Moebius band M = [0,1] x R / ~ where (0,y) ~ (1,-y). Embed n -> (1/(1+|n|), n) for n >= 0 and n -> (1/(1+|n|), -|n|) for n < 0. Define addition and multiplication coordinatewise on M. Prove Z_M is a ring: (a,b) + (c,d) = ((a+c mod 1), b+d with sign from twist). Prove Z_M is not an integral domain: find zero divisors. Prove the twist prime theorem: every Moebius integer n has a unique factorization n = epsilon * p_1^{a_1} * ... * p_k^{a_k} where epsilon = +1 or -1 is the twist, and p_i are ordinary primes. Test: factor 6 = +1 * 2 * 3, -6 = -1 * 2 * 3. Verify multiplication: 2_+ * 3_+ = 6_+ and 2_- * 3_- = 6_+ (two twists cancel). Verify that -1 is prime: if -1 = a*b in Z_M, then a or b must be the twist.
directions.title: Arithmetic on the Moebius Band: A Number System with a Twist

directions.description: There exists a constant δ > 0 such that for every integer n ≥ 2, there exists a finite set P ⊂ ℝ² of n points where the most frequent nonzero distance occurs at least n^(1+δ) times among ordered pairs. This is the core quantitative claim of the paper: the Minkowski grid construction vertically amplifies the one-dimensional Ramanujan estimate for r₂ to produce point sets whose distance multiplicity is superlinear, thereby yielding counterexamples to Erdős's unit distance conjecture under scaling.
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
theorem superlinear_distance_in_minkowski_grid :
    ∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 2 ≤ n →
      ∃ P : Finset (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)),
        P.card = n ∧ ∃ λ : ℝ, 0 < λ ∧
        ((P ×ˢ P).filter (fun pq => pq.1 ≠ pq.2 ∧ dist pq.1 pq.2 = λ)).card ≥ (n : ℝ) ^ (1 + δ)) :=
  by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Construct P as a Minkowski grid over a number field K/ℚ of degree d ≥ 2. Points lie in a scaled lattice derived from the ring of integers of K, so that squared distances correspond to values of the norm form N_{K/ℚ}. The Ramanujan estimate max_{m≤x} r_d(m) ≥ exp(c·log x / log log x) for the number of representations by the norm form, combined with the vertical amplification from dimension 1 to 2, yields the exponent gain δ = δ(d) > 0. The parameter δ arises from the interplay between the degree d and the pigeonhole-type averaging over the grid.
directions.title: Superlinear distance multiplicity in Minkowski grids

directions.description: For any finite subset X of ℝⁿ equipped with the Euclidean metric, the microscopic weighting μ exists and satisfies: μ(x) > 0 if and only if x is a vertex (extreme point) of conv(X), and μ(x) ≤ 0 for every non-extreme point of X. This formalizes the heuristic that the microscopic weighting emphasizes boundary points and assigns greater weight to outlying regions.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem microscopic_weighting_sign_characterization (n : ℕ) (X : Finset (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))) : ∃ (μ : X → ℝ), is_microscopic_weighting μ ∧ ∀ x, μ x > 0 ↔ is_extreme_point x (convexHull ℝ (X : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)))) := by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: First formalize the magnitude weighting w(t) as the solution to the linear system ∑_{y∈X} e^{-td(x,y)} w(y,t) = 1, then define the microscopic weighting as the limit μ(x) = lim_{t→∞} w(x,t). Use the Schoenberg embedding characterization for spaces of strictly negative type, and the energy integral optimization formulation. The sign characterization likely requires analyzing the variational problem: show that minimizing the energy forces positive mass onto extreme points (which are maximally spread) and non-positive mass onto interior points (which are redundant for energy minimization). For the converse direction (non-extreme points get non-positive weight), use the convex combination structure of interior points and the strict negativity of the kernel.
directions.title: Sign Characterization of Microscopic Weighting on Euclidean Subsets

directions.description: The paper proves that μ₂ ≤ 1 + ρ, where μ₂ is the infimum over all infinite sequences of radial cuts of the supremum of the ratio of maximum to minimum portion (adjacent-pair) sizes, and ρ ≈ 0.75488 is the unique real root of x² + x³ = 1 in (0,1). Korsky proved μ₂ ≥ 5/3. The conjecture asserts that the paper's upper bound is tight: μ₂ = 1 + ρ. This would require showing that no cutting strategy can achieve a ratio strictly less than 1 + ρ in the limit, which likely demands a structural impossibility argument about the combinatorics of slice-size configurations.

-- A Portion is the sum of two adjacent slices

A possible approach: (1) characterize the set of achievable slice-size configurations as words over a finite alphabet of size classes, (2) show via a combinatorial/entropy argument that any long word avoiding the forbidden patterns from Proposition 2 must contain a factor whose portion ratio approaches 1 + ρ, or (3) use a potential function argument showing that any deviation from the ρ² : ρ³ splitting rule inevitably creates worse imbalances.
directions.title: Tightness of the adjacent-pair cake-cutting bound: μ₂ = 1 + ρ

directions.description: Erdős repeatedly asked whether there exists an absolute constant c_0 > 0 such that for all sufficiently large x, the number N(x) of odd integers n ≤ x which cannot be written as p + 2^a + 2^b (with p a prime and a, b natural numbers) satisfies N(x) > c_0 * x. This asserts that a positive proportion of odd integers are not of this form, upgrading the current x^{1-o(1)} lower bounds to a positive density.

theorem odd_int_not_p_2a_2b_positive_density :
  ∃ (c₀ : ℝ), c₀ > 0 ∧ ∃ (x₀ : ℕ), ∀ (x : ℕ), x ≥ x₀ →
    (Finset.filter (fun n => Odd n ∧ ¬∃ p a b, Nat.Prime p ∧ n = p + 2^a + 2^b) (Finset.Icc 1 x)).card ≥ ⌈c₀ * x⌉₊ := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Establish that the set of odd integers not representable in this form has positive lower asymptotic density. This likely requires bypassing the exponential bounds produced by covering congruence systems, perhaps by demonstrating that a positive proportion of integers fall into residue classes that are fundamentally excluded by the structure of cyclotomic prime divisors, or by applying additive combinatorics to bound the density of the sumset.
directions.title: Positive Lower Asymptotic Density of Odd Integers Not Representable as p + 2^a + 2^b

directions.description: For every integer r ≥ 2 and real ε > 0, there exists Δ₀ such that for every (r+1)-uniform hypergraph H with girth at least 5 and maximum degree Δ ≥ Δ₀, the list chromatic number χ_ℓ(H) satisfies χ_ℓ(H) ≤ ⌈(1+ε)(rΔ / ln Δ)^(1/r)⌉. This conjecture formalizes the main theorem of the paper, improving Iliopoulos's bound of (1+o(1))r(Δ/ln Δ)^(1/r) by reducing the leading constant from r to r^(1/r) via a semi-random nibble argument combined with a Rosenfeld-style counting completion.
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
theorem list_chromatic_uncrowded_hypergraph {r : ℕ} (hr : r ≥ 2) (ε : ℝ) (hε : ε > 0) : ∃ Δ₀ : ℕ, ∀ Δ ≥ Δ₀, ∀ (H : SimpleHypergraph) (huniform : H.uniform (r + 1)) (hgirth : H.girth ≥ 5) (hdeg : H.max_degree ≤ Δ), H.list_chromatic_number ≤ ⌈(1 + ε) * (r * Δ / Real.log Δ) ^ (1 / r : ℝ)⌉₊ := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Formalize the semi-random nibble in two phases: (1) define the nibble process on the hypergraph with active edge-color constraints, proving concentration of residual degrees via Chernoff-type binomial bounds (requiring Measure Theory / Probability bridges), (2) establish a sparse terminal state condition, (3) complete the coloring via a Rosenfeld-style counting argument (injection from list assignments to proper colorings). The girth ≥ 5 (uncrowded) hypothesis controls dependency structures and should be encoded as a locality condition on the hypergraph's Berge-cycle structure. Start with r = 2 (3-uniform case) to simplify the exponent.
directions.title: List Chromatic Number Bound for Uncrowded Uniform Hypergraphs

directions.description: For every primitive holomorphic newform f of weight k ≥ 4, level N, and nebentypus χ, and for every non-negative integer m, all zeros of the derivative period polynomial P⁽ᵐ⁾_f(z) = Σ_{j=0}^{k-2} C(k-2,j) · Λ⁽ᵐ⁾(f, j+1) · z^j lie on the unit circle, where Λ(f,s) denotes the completed L-function. This confirms and extends the Diamantis–Rolen conjecture to arbitrary level, nebentypus, and derivative order. The core mechanism is a sharp circular sampling theorem: for balanced polynomials p with zeros in Ω_d = {a+ib : a² − b²/(d−1) ≤ d/4}, the centered binomial sample B_d[p] has all zeros on the unit circle.

    {N : ℕ} {k : ℕ} {χ : DirichletCharacter N}
    (hk : k ≥ 4)
    (f : Newform N k χ)
    (hf : f.IsPrimitive)
    (m : ℕ) :
    ∀ z ∈ (derivativePeriodPoly f m hk).roots,
      Complex.abs z = 1 := by
  sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Stage 1: Formalize the sharp circular sampling theorem for balanced polynomials — if p is balanced (p = ω·J(p) with |ω|=1, where J(F)(s) = conj(F(-conj(s)))) and Z(p) ⊆ Ω_{d,δ}, then all zeros of B_{d,δ}[p](z) = Σ C(d,j)·p(δ(j−d/2))·z^j lie on the unit circle, with Ω_{d,δ} maximal. Stage 2: Build completed L-function infrastructure for primitive holomorphic newforms, establishing the functional equation (supplying the balancing symmetry) and the Euler-product zero-free half-plane (placing reflected zeros in the required strip). Stage 3: Apply the sampling theorem with de Bruijn strip contraction and projective HKO theory to transport completed-zero geometry to derivative period polynomial circularity, simplicity, and strict interlacing.
directions.title: Derivative Period Polynomial Unit-Circle Theorem for Primitive Holomorphic Newforms

directions.description: For every elliptic curve E/Q with good supersingular reduction at 2 and square-free conductor, the sharp and flat μ-invariants of Sprung's 2-adic L-functions vanish: μ₂^♯(E,ωⁱ) = μ₂^♭(E,ωⁱ) = 0 for all i ∈ {0,1}. This is a 2-adic supersingular analogue of Greenberg's μ=0 conjecture. Its truth would render the λ-invariant difference formula in the paper unconditional, extending Matsuno-type formulas completely to the supersingular setting at p=2.
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem sharp_flat_mu_vanish_supersingular_2 (E : EllipticCurve ℚ) (h_ss : GoodSupersingularReductionAt E 2) (h_sf : SquareFree (conductor E)) (i : Fin 2) : muInvariant (signedPadicLFunction E 2 SignType.sharp i) = 0 ∧ muInvariant (signedPadicLFunction E 2 SignType.flat i) = 0 := by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Establish the vanishing of algebraic μ-invariants for the signed (♯/♭) Selmer groups via control theorems and the structure of torsion in Mordell–Weil groups over the cyclotomic Z₂-extension. Then invoke the Iwasawa main conjecture for supersingular primes (proved by Kobayashi, Sprung, etc.) to transfer vanishing from the algebraic to the analytic side. The supersingular condition at 2, combined with square-free conductor, constrains the 2-adic torsion structure sufficiently to force μ=0.
directions.title: Vanishing of sharp/flat 2-adic μ-invariants for semistable supersingular elliptic curves

directions.description: Ramanujan's constant e^{pi*sqrt(163)} is remarkably close to an integer: it equals 262537412640768743.99999999999925... — just 7.5 * 10^{-13} away from 262537412640768744. This is not a coincidence: 163 is the largest Heegner number, and the near-integer property follows from the j-function and the fact that Q(sqrt(-163)) has class number 1. But 163 appears EVERYWHERE: it is prime, it is the smallest p such that Q(sqrt(-p)) has class number 1 and p > 2, it is a Chen prime, a lucky prime, a strongly prime, and the 38th prime. Conjecture: 163 is the unique integer n such that e^{pi*sqrt(n)} is within 10^{-6} of an integer. More generally, the Heegner numbers (1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43, 67, 163) are exactly the n for which Q(sqrt(-n)) has class number 1, and e^{pi*sqrt(n)} is near-integer for each. The 'magic' of 163 is that it is the LAST Heegner number — the final class number 1 imaginary quadratic field. Test: prove that e^{pi*sqrt(n)} is within 10^{-6} of an integer only for Heegner numbers. Compute e^{pi*sqrt(67)} and e^{pi*sqrt(43)} and verify near-integer behavior. Prove that 163 is the largest Heegner number (Stark-Heegner theorem). Impact: 163 is not magic — it is the climax of a deep theorem in algebraic number theory. The near-integer property of e^{pi*sqrt(163)} is the shadow of the class number 1 condition.
directions.proof_strategy: State the Stark-Heegner theorem: the imaginary quadratic fields Q(sqrt(-d)) with class number 1 are exactly d = 1, 2, 3, 7, 11, 19, 43, 67, 163. Prove e^{pi*sqrt(d)} is near-integer for each Heegner number: by the j-function expansion, j((1+sqrt(-d))/2) is an algebraic integer, and e^{pi*sqrt(d)} = (j/1728 + ... )^{1/3} * 12. For d = 163, j((1+sqrt(-163))/2) = -640320^3, so e^{pi*sqrt(163)} = 640320^3 + 744 - error. Prove uniqueness: for non-Heegner d, the class number h(-d) >= 2, so j((1+sqrt(-d))/2) has degree h(-d) >= 2 over Q, and e^{pi*sqrt(d)} is not near-integer. Test: compute e^{pi*sqrt(d)} for d = 1,2,3,7,11,19,43,67,163 and verify near-integer behavior. Compute for d = 5,6,10,14 to verify non-near-integer behavior.
directions.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of the Number 163

directions.description: The shadowing lemma says that near an approximate orbit of a chaotic system, there exists a true orbit. In other words, every 'almost correct' trajectory of a chaotic map has a 'truly correct' trajectory nearby. This means that numerical errors in chaotic simulations are not bugs — they are SHADOWS of real trajectories. Conjecture: Every program that computes a chaotic map f: R^n -> R^n has the property that its floating-point output is shadowed by a true orbit of f. More precisely, for every epsilon > 0, there exists delta > 0 such that if x_0, x_1, ..., x_N is a delta-pseudo-orbit (|x_{n+1} - f(x_n)| < delta for all n), then there exists a true orbit y_0, y_1, ..., y_N with |x_n - y_n| < epsilon for all n. The shadowing time N(epsilon, delta) grows at most polynomially in 1/delta for hyperbolic maps. Test: implement the logistic map f(x) = 4x(1-x) in floating-point and compute 10^6 iterations. For each floating-point orbit, use binary search to find the shadowing true orbit. Verify that the shadowing distance is at most 10^{-10} for floating-point precision 10^{-16}. Impact: numerical chaos is not error — it is a computable shadow of mathematical truth. Your computer's rounding errors are tracing out REAL orbits of the chaotic system.
directions.proof_strategy: State the Anosov shadowing lemma: for a hyperbolic map f on a compact manifold, for every epsilon > 0 there exists delta > 0 such that every delta-pseudo-orbit is epsilon-shadowed by a true orbit. Prove the conjecture: every floating-point computation of f is a delta-pseudo-orbit with delta = machine epsilon. By shadowing, there exists a true orbit within epsilon. The shadowing distance epsilon is at most C * delta^(1/s) where s is the expansion rate and C depends on the map. For the logistic map at r=4, s = 4 and epsilon = O(delta^{1/4}). Compute the shadowing orbit: given floating-point orbit x_0, ..., x_N, define y_0 = x_0 and y_{n+1} = f(y_n). Then |y_n - x_n| <= C * delta * (s^n - 1)/(s - 1). For N = 10^6 and delta = 10^{-16}, epsilon <= C * 10^{-16} * (4^{10^6} - 1)/3 which is too large. But for the shadowing lemma, we get epsilon = O(delta^{1/4}) = O(10^{-4}). Test: verify with numerical computation.
directions.title: Chaos as a Computable Shadow: The Shadowing Lemma for Real Programs

directions.description: The Monster group M is the largest sporadic simple group, with order 2^46 * 3^20 * 5^9 * 7^6 * 11^2 * 13^3 * 17 * 19 * 23 * 29 * 31 * 41 * 47 * 59 * 71 (approximately 8 * 10^{53}). Monstrous moonshine says that the coefficients of the j-function encode the dimensions of representations of M. But the j-function is just the TIP of the iceberg. Conjecture: The full moonshine correspondence associates to each conjugacy class g in M a McKay-Thompson series T_g(q) = sum a_n(g) q^n that is a modular function of a specific level, and the product over all g in M of T_g(q) equals a modular form of weight |M|/24 that encodes the complete character table of M. The secret message: the Monster group IS a modular form, and every property of M (its order, its character table, its maximal subgroups) can be read off from the q-expansion of this product. Test: compute the first 100 coefficients of T_g(q) for each conjugacy class of M and verify they match the known character values. Prove that the product of all T_g(q) converges to a modular form. Impact: the Monster is not just connected to modular forms — it IS a modular form. The 194 conjugacy classes of M correspond to 194 modular forms, and their product encodes everything.
directions.proof_strategy: State the moonshine conjecture (proved by Borcherds): each conjugacy class g of M has a McKay-Thompson series T_g(q) that is a Hauptmodul of genus 0 for a specific modular curve. Extend: define the Monster product P(q) = prod_{g in Conj(M)} T_g(q)^{1/|C(g)|} where C(g) is the conjugacy class. Prove P(q) converges: log P(q) = sum_g (1/|C(g)|) * log T_g(q) = sum_g sum_n (1/|C(g)|) * a_n(g)/n * q^n. Each term is bounded by |a_n(g)|/n * |q|^n which is O(n^{3/2}) by Deligne's bound. Prove P(q) is a modular form of weight |M|/24 = 8 * 10^{53}/24 by checking it transforms correctly under each level. Test: compute P(q) mod q^{100} and compare with the character table of M.
directions.title: The Monster Group's Secret Message: Moonshine Beyond the j-Function

directions.description: Einstein showed that gravity is the curvature of spacetime. But WHY does spacetime curve? Conjecture: Spacetime IS a quantum error-correcting code, and gravity IS the syndrome of that code. The code is a [[n,k,d]] stabilizer code where n = number of Planck areas on a spatial slice, k = number of logical qubits (which equals the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy S = A/4G in natural units), and d = code distance (which equals the minimal geodesic length through the bulk). The key identity: S(A) = Area(gamma_A) / (4G) is EXACTLY the quantum Singleton bound n - k <= 2(d-1) rearranged as k = n - 2d + 2 = A/(4G) when n = A/l_P^2 and d = L/(2l_P). This means the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy formula is a quantum coding theorem, and the holographic principle is a coding constraint. Test: for AdS_3 with boundary CFT_2, the code is a [[n, k, d]] = [[L/l_P, S, L/(2l_P)]] code. Verify that the Singleton bound n - k <= 2(d-1) becomes L/l_P - S <= L/l_P - 1, which simplifies to S >= 1 (trivially true). The NON-TRIVIAL content is that the Ryu-Takayanagi formula S = A/(4G) is the exact quantum information identity. Impact: spacetime is not curved by matter — spacetime IS a code, and matter IS a syndrome. Gravity is not a force; it's error correction.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the spacetime code: qubits = Planck areas on a spatial slice, stabilizers = boundary terms of the Einstein-Hilbert action, logical operators = bulk geodesics. Prove the Bekenstein-Hawking identity: S = A/(4G) equals the quantum coding bound k = n - 2d + 2. Derive: n = A/l_P^2 (number of Planck areas), k = S = A/(4G) (logical qubits from Bekenstein-Hawking), d = L/(2l_P) (distance from minimal geodesic). Check: k = n - 2d + 2 = A/l_P^2 - L/l_P + 2. For AdS_3, A = 2*pi*R and L = 2*pi*R, so k = 2*pi*R/l_P^2 - 2*pi*R/l_P + 2 = 2*pi*R/(l_P^2) * (1 - l_P/R) + 2. For R >> l_P, this gives k ≈ 2*pi*R/l_P^2 = A/l_P^2 which matches S = A/(4G). The correction terms are quantum corrections of order l_P/R. Test: verify for AdS_3 with BTZ black holes.
directions.title: Gravity from Information: Spacetime as a Quantum Error-Correcting Code

directions.description: The supremum of achievable vertical amplification parameters δ in the paper's main theorem equals 1/3. Precisely: for every ε > 0, there exist infinitely many n ∈ ℕ and finite sets P ⊂ ℝ² with |P| = n such that for every A ⊆ P with |A| ≥ 2, the maximum distance multiplicity μ(A) ≥ |A|² / n^(2/3 + ε). This would be optimal given the O(n^{4/3}) Szemerédi–Trotter upper bound on unit distances, which forces δ ≤ 1/3. The paper establishes existence of some δ > 0; this conjectures δ can approach 1/3 via increasingly high-degree number field constructions.

The key is to show that as the degree d grows, the amplification factor δ_d approaches 1/3, matching the Szemerédi–Trotter barrier. A potential approach involves cyclotomic fields or more general number fields where the class number and unit structure provide increasingly many representations.
directions.title: Optimal Vertical Amplification Conjecture for Planar Point Sets

directions.description: For any fixed integer $r \ge 2$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, every sufficiently large finite uncrowded $(r+1)$-uniform hypergraph of maximum degree $\Delta$ has list chromatic number at most $(1+\varepsilon)(r\Delta/\log\Delta)^{1/r}$. This captures the paper's main theorem, improving the leading constant from $r$ to $r^{1/r}$ over prior work by Iliopoulos.

Establish a binomial degree bound to maintain invariants during the nibble phase, then apply a Rosenfeld-style counting argument to complete the coloring in the sparse terminal state.

directions.description: Conjecture: Let ρ be the unique real root of x^2 + x^3 = 1 in (0,1). Define μ₂ as the infimum over all infinite sequences of radial cuts of a circular cake (as described in the paper) of the supremum over time of the ratio between the largest and smallest portion (adjacent pair of slices). Then μ₂ = 1+ρ.

For the lower bound μ₂ ≥ 1+ρ, one would analyze the combinatorial constraints on slice sizes imposed by the cutting rule and show that any infinite sequence must eventually produce a portion whose size ratio is at least 1+ρ. This can be approached by modeling the slice sizes as a multiplicative walk on the set {1, ρ, ρ², ρ³} and using a potential function or invariant derived from the forbidden factors in Proposition~O\\ref{propNoRepeat} to bound the frequency of large slices relative to small ones, ultimately yielding the desired ratio.
directions.title: Optimality of the 1+ρ bound for the maximum-to-minimum portion ratio in the iterative cake-cutting process

directions.description: The partial dominating set value function |N[S]| (number of vertices dominated by a set S) cannot be expressed as an FO Value expression with quantifier-free correction terms over the vocabulary of graphs. Concretely: for every unary weight function w : V(G) → ℕ and every quantifier-free formula φ(x₁,...,xₘ) over the vocabulary {E}, there exists a graph G and a finite set S ⊆ V(G) such that |N_G[S]| ≠ (Σ_{v ∈ S} w(v)) − |{(v₁,...,vₘ) ∈ Sᵐ : G ⊨ φ(v₁,...,vₘ)}|. This contrasts with Partial Vertex Cover, which the paper shows is a quantifier-free FO Value instance via the identity |{e : e ∩ S ≠ ∅}| = Σ_{v ∈ S} deg(v) − |E(G[S])|, where the correction term E(x,y) is quantifier-free. The dominating set value requires counting vertices outside S that are adjacent to multiple vertices in S, necessitating existential quantification over vertices not in the selected tuple.

      (hφ : φ.is_quantifier_free)
      (w : V(G) → ℕ),
    ∃ (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (S : Finset (Fin n)),
      (S.card = k) ∧
      (G.neighborFinset S ∪ S).card ≠
        (∑ v in S, w v) -
        (Finset.card <| S.attach.filter (fun ⟨x, _⟩ =>
          S.attach.filter (fun ⟨y, _⟩ =>
            φ_satisfies G x.val y.val φ)))
-- where φ_satisfies evaluates the quantifier-free formula φ
-- on the induced subgraph restricted to the tuple variables
directions.proof_strategy: Construct a family of graphs G_k parameterized by k such that for any quantifier-free formula φ with m free variables and any unary weight w, one can find a set S in some G_k where the quantifier-free FO Value decomposition fails. The key insight is that quantifier-free formulas over the tuple variables can only detect local adjacency patterns among selected vertices, but |N[S]| depends on the number of external vertices adjacent to multiple tuple elements—a global property requiring existential quantification over vertices outside S. A candidate proof uses Hanf-locality of quantifier-free FO: two tuples with the same atomic type in G yield the same correction value, but can dominate different numbers of external vertices, breaking the decomposition.
directions.title: Inexpressibility of Partial Dominating Set as Quantifier-Free FO Value

directions.description: For every integer k ≥ 3, there exists a constant c_k > 0 such that every C_{2k}-free graph with average degree at least c_k · h contains an induced subdivision of K_h. This conjectures that the polylogarithmic factor in the authors' bound of Ω_k(h log^5 h) can be eliminated, making the threshold purely linear in h, which would be tight up to the constant factor.

Key insight: C_{2k}-free graphs have stronger pseudo-random properties than currently exploited, and more careful use of the dependent random choice or balanced-supergraph techniques could yield path systems that directly give induced subdivisions without the logarithmic overhead from iterative refinement.
directions.title: Linear threshold for induced clique subdivisions in even-cycle-free graphs

directions.description: For P(X) = X² + 1, the number of pairs (n, m) with 1 ≤ n < m ≤ N such that (n²+1)(m²+1) is a perfect square is O(logᴬ N) for some absolute constant A ≥ 0. This is equivalent to the variance of the extended Rademacher partial sum ∑_{n≤N} f(n²+1) satisfying Var = N + O(logᴬ N), meaning the off-diagonal contribution is negligible. The equation (n²+1)(m²+1) = k² reduces via Gaussian integer norms to the Pythagorean-type condition (nm−1)² + (n+m)² = k², which for fixed n yields Pell equations whose solutions grow exponentially, giving only O(log N) solutions per n. The conjecture asserts the total across all n ≤ N remains polylogarithmic.

        nm.1 < nm.2 ∧ nm.2 ≤ N ∧
        ∃ k : ℕ, (nm.1^2 + 1) * (nm.2^2 + 1) = k^2)

Use the structure of solutions to Pell equations parametrized by fundamental units in Q(√(−(n²+1))) and related fields. The key is to show that for each n, the number of m ≤ N with (n²+1)(m²+1) = □ is O(log N), and then sum over n using that n²+1 has few representations as norms from quadratic extensions. The Gaussian integer factorization (n²+1)(m²+1) = |(n+i)(m+i)|² = |(nm−1)+(n+m)i|² transforms the problem into counting Pythagorean representations, where height bounds on rational points control the count.
directions.title: Polylogarithmic Paucity of Square Products of Shifted Squares

directions.description: For any ε > 0, there exist effectively computable constants C(ε) > 0 and Q₀(ε) > 0 such that: if for every primitive quadratic Dirichlet character χ with conductor q ≥ Q₀(ε), all non-real zeros ρ of L(s,χ) satisfy Re(ρ) ≤ 1 - C(ε)/log(q), then there is at most one such character χ whose associated L-function has a real zero β in the interval [1 - q^(-ε), 1). This formalizes the paper's main result that excluding non-real zeros from a shrinking neighborhood of s=1 allows a significant refinement of Page's theorem.

  (∃! χ : Σ q, DirichletCharacter q, χ.2.IsQuadratic ∧ χ.2.IsPrimitive ∧ χ.1 ≥ Q₀ ∧
    ∃ β : ℝ, β ∈ Set.Icc (1 - (χ.1 : ℝ) ^ (-ε)) 1 ∧ IsZeroOfDirichletLFn (β : ℂ) χ.2) ∨

    ∃ β : ℝ, β ∈ Set.Icc (1 - (χ.1 : ℝ) ^ (-ε)) 1 ∧ IsZeroOfDirichletLFn (β : ℂ) χ.2) := by

Key ingredients include logarithmic derivative estimates for L-functions, the Deuring-Heilbronn phenomenon, and effective bounds from the geometry of the zeros. Formalization would proceed by first establishing the effective constants, then the conditional zero-free region, and finally the uniqueness of the exceptional zero.

directions.description: For the free Catalan structure (C, e, λ, ⊕) satisfying the unique decomposition property from Definition 1, the involution h = rev ∘ corev ∘ rev restricted to level C_n has exactly C_n fixed points, where C_n = (2n choose n)/(n+1) is the n-th Catalan number. This asserts that the fixed-point enumerator of h matches the Catalan generating function.

Define rev and corev by structural recursion on the first-return and last-return decompositions respectively. Prove h = rev ∘ corev ∘ rev is involutive. Then establish the fixed-point count by constructing an explicit bijection between Fix(h|_{C_n}) and binary trees on n internal nodes, using the characterization that t is a fixed point iff rev(t) = corev(t).

directions.description: An extension of the Colorful Carathéodory theorem to convex cones: given $r \ge d$ pairwise disjoint sets of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$ such that the origin is in the convex cone generated by each set, there exists a colorful transversal whose convex cone also contains the origin.

directions.description: Every exotic Diophantine triple {a, b, c} of distinct nonzero polynomials in ℝ[X] with at least one nonconstant element must contain the element 1. That is, if a+1, b+1, c+1, ab+1, ac+1, bc+1, and abc+1 are all perfect squares in ℝ[X], and at least one of a, b, c is nonconstant, then one of a, b, c equals 1.

directions.description: For any prime p, any p-adic optimization ℓ: ℚ_p^n → ℝ_{≥0} ∪ {∞}, any E ∈ ℕ, and any finite set C ⊆ (ℤ/p^Eℤ)^n, if (1) for all c ∈ dom(ℓ) \ π_E^{-1}(C) there exists d ∈ C with ℓ(d) < ℓ(c), and (2) for all c ∈ π_E^{-1}(C), ℓ(π_E(c)) ≤ ℓ(c), then ℓ is (E,C)-reducible: every optimal solution of OP(ℓ,C) is optimal for OP(ℓ), and every optimal solution c of OP(ℓ) satisfies c ∈ π_E^{-1}(C) with π_E(c) optimal for OP(ℓ,C). This is the key structural proposition enabling the generalized Baker forcing method.

Formalization requires: (a) defining ℚ_p and the projection π_E: ℚ_p^n → (ℤ/p^Eℤ)^n, (b) defining p-adic optimizations as partial maps ℚ_p^n → ℝ_{≥0} ∪ {∞}, (c) defining (E,C)-reducibility and the restricted optimization problem OP(ℓ,C), then proving the two optimality conditions follow from the hypotheses.

directions.description: For any integer $k \ge 4$, there exists a constant $C_k > 0$ such that for all positive integers $N$, the minimum modulus of a non-vanishing sum of $k$ $N$-th roots of unity satisfies $f(k, N) \le C_k \cdot N^{-k/4}$. This would generalize Myerson's asymptotic bound $f(k,N) \le N^{-k/4+o_N(1)}$ for even $k$ and even $N$ to all $k \ge 4$ and all $N$, vastly improving upon the logarithmic growth of the exponent $\alpha_k$ established in the paper.

directions.description: For every Turán graph T(n, r) with r ≥ 4 and n ≥ 4r, and for every edge e of T(n, r), the Seidel energy strictly increases upon deletion: E_S(T(n, r) − e) > E_S(T(n, r)). This is Theorem 1.2 of the paper, resolving a problem of Tian et al., but its formalization requires building the entire theory of Seidel matrices, Seidel energy, Turán graphs, and the reduced-order spectral machinery for blow-up graphs—a substantial formalization undertaking.

Establish the reduced-order spectral criterion that reduces the Seidel energy comparison to eigenvalue analysis of a smaller matrix whose order depends only on the number of partite sets. Apply this criterion to the Turán graph case with r ≥ 4 and n ≥ 4r, verifying the inequality via explicit eigenvalue computation on the reduced matrix.

directions.description: Every connected vertex-transitive digraph on n ≥ 1 vertices contains a directed cycle of length at least ⌈√n⌉. This is the natural directed analogue of Babai's 1979 theorem for undirected vertex-transitive graphs, and strengthens the paper's asymptotic Ω(√n) lower bound to an explicit constant of 1.

The proof likely uses the orbit-stabilizer theorem and group-theoretic analysis of the automorphism group acting on the digraph to find a long directed cycle. Key steps: (1) formalize vertex-transitive digraphs and their automorphism groups, (2) establish that connected vertex-transitive digraphs on n vertices have minimum out-degree ≥ 1 and use orbit structure to find cycles, (3) combine the orbit counting with cycle-finding arguments to extract a directed cycle of length ≥ ⌈√n⌉. The existence result (digraphs missing n/12 vertices) provides the complementary upper bound context.

directions.description: We conjecture that for the critical case ε=1/2, the maximal anti-Ramsey function for P_4 admits an exact quadratic lower bound with a computable constant. Specifically, we propose that χ_S(n, (n choose 2) - ⌊n^{3/2}⌋, P_4) > (1/8 - o(1))·n² as n → ∞, where the constant 1/8 arises from the induced matching structure in graphs with minimum degree (1/2 + o(1))n. This conjecture addresses the sharpness of the phase transition at ε=1/2 and would require establishing both the lower bound and matching upper bound to determine the exact asymptotic behavior.
domain_bridges: Connections between induced matchings and rainbow colorings
Relationship to the Erdős-Gallai theorem on paths
Bridge between extremal graph theory and Ramsey-type colorings
Threshold phenomena in sparse-dense graph transitions
directions.lean_theorem_stub: theorem sharp_antiramsey_P4_threshold : ∀ ε : ℝ, ε = 1/2 → (∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in filter.at_top, ∃ c : ℝ, c = 1/8 ∧ χ_S (n, binomial n 2 - ⌊n^(2-ε)⌋, P_4) > c * n^2)
directions.proof_strategy: The proof would require three main components: (1) Constructive lower bound via explicit graph families showing χ_S(n, (n choose 2) - ⌊n^{3/2}⌋, P_4) ≥ (1/8 - o(1))·n² using induced matching analysis; (2) Upper bound construction demonstrating that no more than (1/8 + o(1))·n² colors are needed; (3) Stability analysis around the minimum degree threshold (1/2)n to verify the exact constant. The approach involves analyzing the structure of graphs missing Θ(n^{3/2}) edges and their P_4 rainbow colorings through induced matching decompositions.
directions.title: Sharp Threshold and Exact Constant for P_4 Anti-Ramsey Number at ε=1/2

directions.description: The Kaneko-Zagier conjecture posits that there exists a well-defined ring isomorphism between the quotient ring of multiple zeta values Z / zeta(2)Z and the ring of finite multiple zeta values Z_A. Specifically, the map sending a symmetric multiple zeta value zeta_S(k) to its corresponding finite multiple zeta value zeta_A(k) is well-defined and preserves the algebraic structures, meaning any Q-linear relation among SMZVs corresponds to an identical relation among FMZVs.

Prove that the kernel of the natural projection from MZVs to SMZVs is generated by zeta(2), and show that the map sending SMZVs to FMZVs respects all algebraic relations, thereby establishing the ring isomorphism.
directions.title: Kaneko-Zagier Conjecture for Symmetric and Finite MZVs

directions.description: For the odd Euler ensemble at cutoff N, the positive spectral moments M^{odd}_{s,+}(N; n) satisfy the precise limit: lim_{N → ∞} √(2N/π) · M^{odd}_{s,+}(N; n) / |n|^s = ζ(s) for all real s > 1 and nonzero integers n. This identifies the Riemann zeta function as the spectral moment generating function emerging from the continuum limit of the marginally stable turbulent attractor, bridging the arithmetic structure of reduced rational angles p/q with the Lyapunov stability analysis of incompressible Navier–Stokes turbulence.

The key step is expressing M^{odd}_{s,+}(N; n) as a sum over coprime pairs (p, q) with q odd, weighted by |n/q|^s, and showing the normalization √(2N/π) converts the discrete sum to ζ(s) via Euler product or Dirichlet series techniques available in Mathlib's number theory layer.
directions.title: Odd Euler Ensemble Spectral Moment Zeta Convergence

directions.description: Every finitely generated virtually nilpotent group has finite twin-width. This conjecture provides a positive structural guarantee for the combinatorial parameter of twin-width from the algebraic assumption of virtual nilpotence, complementing the paper's negative result that finite twin-width does not imply accessibility. Specifically, if Γ is a finitely generated group containing a nilpotent subgroup of finite index, then every Cayley graph of Γ has finite twin-width (i.e., the supremum of twin-widths of finite induced subgraphs is bounded). The proof would proceed by: (1) establishing that Z^n has finite twin-width by bounding the twin-width of subgraphs of the n-dimensional grid, (2) showing that torsion-free finitely generated nilpotent groups embed as discrete cocompact subgroups of nilpotent Lie groups, yielding quasi-isometric embeddings into R^m whose integer lattice Z^m has finite twin-width, and (3) applying the quasi-isometric invariance of twin-width for bounded-degree graphs (Twin-width VII, Bonnet et al.) together with finite-index arguments for the virtual case.
domain_bridges: Nilpotent group structure theory ↔ grid graph twin-width bounds
Quasi-isometric invariance of twin-width ↔ geometric group theory invariants
Cayley graph combinatorics ↔ Lie group embedding theorems (Mal'cev)

    HasFiniteTwinWidth G :=

    -- 1. Reduce to torsion-free case via finite-index arguments
    -- 2. Embed nilpotent group into Z^m via Mal'cev coordinates
    -- 3. Transfer twin-width bound from Z^m using QI-invariance
    sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Step 1: Prove the n-dimensional integer grid Z^n (as a Cayley graph with standard generators) has twin-width at most n+1, by constructing explicit contraction sequences for finite grid subgraphs that maintain bounded red degree. Step 2: Show that every torsion-free finitely generated nilpotent group N admits a discrete cocompact embedding into its Mal'cev completion (a simply-connected nilpotent Lie group), so that N is quasi-isometric to R^m equipped with a nilpotent Lie group metric, and hence N is quasi-isometric to a finite-index subgroup of Z^m (via the integer lattice). Step 3: Apply the quasi-isometric invariance of finite twin-width for bounded-degree graphs (Twin-width VII) to conclude that N has finite twin-width. Step 4: Extend to virtually nilpotent groups: if G has a nilpotent subgroup H of finite index, then G is quasi-isometric to H, and since H has finite twin-width by Step 3, so does G.
directions.title: Finite Twin-Width of Virtually Nilpotent Groups

directions.description: The theta series of any even positive definite unimodular lattice of rank 8 equals the Eisenstein series E₄. Concretely, for every positive integer n, the number of vectors of norm n in such a lattice equals 240·σ₃(n), where σ₃(n) = Σ_{d|n} d³. This is the foundational special case of the classical Siegel-Weil formula, connecting the theta series of a lattice to an Eisenstein series, and reduces to verifying that the Fourier coefficients of θ_L coincide with those of E₄.

This strengthens the paper's theorem that every bipartite {-1,0,1}-diagonalizable graph is regular, and if true, would provide a complete structural characterization connecting the {-1,0,1}-diagonalizability property to classical complete bipartite graph structure.

directions.description: For all positive integers k ≥ 2, n ≥ 1, and 1 ≤ j ≤ n, the symmetric function Δ_{e_j} G(k,n) is Schur positive (i.e., expands with nonnegative coefficients in ℕ[q,t] in the Schur basis) if and only if k divides n, where G(k,n) = Σ_{λ⊢n, λ₁<k} m_λ is the Petrie symmetric function and Δ_{e_j} is the Bergeron–Garsia delta operator applied to e_j. This extends the paper's main result for ∇ = Δ_{e_n} (and its iterates ∇^r) to all elementary symmetric function inputs of the delta operator, establishing that the divisibility criterion governs Schur positivity uniformly across the entire family of delta operators.

Diagonal harmonics and nabla operator theory

For the converse (k∤n ⟹ not Schur positive): extend the sign-analysis techniques from the paper's nabla case to general Δ_{e_j} by tracking the leading negative Schur coefficients in the Macdonald polynomial expansion of G(k,n) under the delta eigenvalue action, showing that the divisibility obstruction propagates through all delta operators.

directions.description: For Levenshtein's sequence reconstruction problem with insertion errors, the paper proves the surprising fact that N_q^m(n,1) = N_q^{nm}(n,1) for all alphabet size q and word length n—that is, the minimum number of channels required for unambiguous reconstruction is identical whether repeated outputs are tracked as a multiset or as an unordered set, when exactly one insertion occurs per channel. The conjecture proposes that this equality extends to all insertion counts t >= 1: N_q^m(n,t) = N_q^{nm}(n,t) for all q >= 2, n >= 1, t >= 1.

  induction t with
  | zero => simp at ht
  | succ t ih => sorry
directions.proof_strategy: Proceed by induction on t, leveraging the t=1 base case proven in the paper. For the inductive step, analyze how the multiset and non-multiset intersection structures of insertion balls decompose when composing t insertions as a sequence of single insertions. The key difficulty is showing that the overlap multiplicities from repeated error patterns cannot create a distinction between the multiset and non-multiset models even when t > 1. A combinatorial double-counting argument on the equivalence classes of insertion error patterns producing identical outputs may suffice.
directions.title: Equality of Multiset and Non-Multiset Reconstruction Numbers for All Insertion Counts

Specifically, for any Schwartz function f : ℝ^n → ℝ with Fourier transform supported in (-1,1)^n, the family-average of ∑_{distinct i₁,...,i_n} f(θ_{i₁},...,θ_{i_n}) over normalized zero angles θ of L(u,χ_D) converges to ∫_{[0,1]^n} f(x) · W_{n,USp(2g)}(x) dx, where W_{n,USp(2g)} is the symplectic n-level density kernel.

directions.description: For every positive integer m and every 0 < α < 1/2, there exists a constant C(m,α) > 0 such that for all odd prime powers q and all subsets E ⊆ F_q^{2m}, if |E| ≥ C(m,α) · q^m then the set of nonzero quadratic distances Δ_Q^×(E) = {Q(x−y) : x,y ∈ E} ∩ F_q^× has size greater than α(q−1), where Q(x) = x₁² + ⋯ + x_{2m}². This asserts that subsets of F_q^{2m} of size proportional to q^m determine a positive proportion of all possible nonzero distances, which is the sharp threshold predicted by the Erdős–Falconer conjecture. The current paper achieves this conditionally on a Kloosterman anti-concentration conjecture, and unconditionally achieves the weaker q^{m+1/2} threshold.
