theorem erdos_falconer_even_dim_conjecture {m : ℕ} (α : ℝ)
    (hm : 1 ≤ m) (hα : 0 < α) (hα' : α < 1 / 2) :
    ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ (p : ℕ) [Fact (Nat.Prime p)] (hodd : Odd p),
    ∀ (E : Finset (Fin (2 * m) → ZMod p)),
    (E.card : ℝ) ≥ C * (p : ℝ) ^ m →
    let Q := fun (x y : Fin (2 * m) → ZMod p) =>
      ∑ i, (x i - y i) * (x i - y i)
    let D := (Finset.univ : Finset (ZMod p)).erase 0 |>.filter
      fun d => ∃ x ∈ E, ∃ y ∈ E, Q x y = d
    (D.card : ℝ) > α * (p - 1) :=
  by sorry
directions.proof_strategy: The paper's semidefinite Delsarte framework reduces the conjecture to a uniform L¹ anti-concentration statement for positive convex combinations of classical Kloosterman sums. A complete proof requires either (1) establishing the Kloosterman anti-concentration conjecture—that positive convex combinations of Kloosterman sums K_q(a·t) cannot concentrate in L¹ beyond a universal lower bound proportional to 1/√q—or (2) an entirely new method bypassing the Delsarte/LP framework. The unconditional q^{m+1/2} threshold follows from a second-moment bound on Kloosterman sums (Weil bound), but improving to q^m requires overcoming the fundamental barrier that individual Kloosterman columns can nearly cancel.
directions.title: Erdős–Falconer Distance Conjecture in Even Finite Field Dimensions

Although recent breakthroughs have established the first finite upper bounds on the chromatic number of t-perfect graphs (currently 186), a wide gap remains between the lower bound of 4 and the upper bound, making this a central open problem in polyhedral combinatorics.

directions.title: t-Perfect Graph 4-Colorability Conjecture

directions.description: For every loopless matroid M on finite ground set E and every Feichtner–Yuzvinsky building set G containing the top flat E, the K-polynomial of the integral tangent class T^Z_{M,G} ∈ K_Z(M,G) equals the Hilbert series of the Chow ring A*(M,G). Concretely, P^K(T^Z_{M,G}, t) = Hilb(A*(M,G), t) as polynomials in Z[t]. This is the central P^K=Hilb identity (Theorem A, property 2) of the paper, connecting the K-theoretic tangent class to the cohomological Hilbert series.

Construct the integral tangent class via the quotient/theta-machinery of Sections 4-5. Then prove P^K=Hilb by establishing that the K-ring Chern character ch_K maps T^Z_{M,G} to the Todd class whose pushforward recovers the Hilbert series, mirroring the classical HRR argument adapted to the combinatorial setting.

directions.description: For any subset A ⊆ [N] containing no harmonic triple (distinct a, b, c ∈ A with 2/a = 1/b + 1/c), the density |A|/N → 0 as N → ∞. Formally: ∀ ε > 0, ∃ N₀, ∀ N ≥ N₀, every A ⊆ {1,...,N} with no harmonic triple satisfies |A| ≤ ε·N. This is the reciprocal analogue of Roth's theorem on 3-AP-free sets, posed as Question 1 in the paper. The paper's construction yields sets of size ≫ N·exp(−C√(log log N)), so a positive resolution would need new upper-bound techniques beyond Roth-type methods, since the reciprocal map x ↦ 1/x is not additive.

The window encodes an affine plane $w + \langle u_1, u_2 \rangle$ via a triple of mixed affine points and direction classes (e.g., $(w, [u_1], [u_2])$ or $(w, w+u_1, w+u_2)$). This extends the paper's construction which currently holds for $n \ge 4$.

directions.description: The paper proves that every circular Hessenberg pair satisfies the tridiagonal relations (Lee's conjecture). The converse remains open: among all Hessenberg pairs on a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space, exactly the circular ones satisfy the tridiagonal relations. That is, a Hessenberg pair (A, A*) satisfies the tridiagonal relations if and only if it is circular (i.e., each acts on an eigenbasis of the other in a circular Hessenberg fashion, meaning the top-right corner entry is nonzero and every other entry above the superdiagonal is zero).

directions.proof_strategy: The forward direction is the content of the paper (proving Lee's conjecture). For the converse, suppose a Hessenberg pair satisfies the tridiagonal relations. Use the tridiagonal relations to derive constraints on the matrix entries of each operator acting on the other's eigenbasis. Show that the vanishing conditions above the superdiagonal (except the top-right corner) and the nonvanishing of the top-right corner follow from the tridiagonal relations combined with the Hessenberg structure. This may involve analyzing the recurrence relations imposed by the tridiagonal relations on the entries of the Hessenberg matrices and showing that non-circular Hessenberg pairs violate these relations.
directions.title: Circular Hessenberg pairs are characterized by the tridiagonal relations

directions.description: Formalize that every finite simple subcubic outerplanar graph admits a crumby coloring: a red-blue vertex partition where the blue vertices induce a subgraph of maximum degree at most one, and the red vertices induce a subgraph with minimum degree at least one and no induced path on four vertices (P₄). This resolves the Barát–Blázsik–Damásdi conjecture and extends their result from 2-connected to all subcubic outerplanar graphs. The proof introduces a rooted grammatical decomposition of subcubic outerplanar graphs into rooted branches and two-terminal path fragments, extends crumby colorings to crumby-admissible colorings that permit temporary defects at boundary vertices, and reduces the inductive verification to checking an explicit finite family of certificates.
domain_bridges: Graph minor theory ↔ constrained 2-colorability (outerplanarity as a forbidden-minor condition enabling the grammatical decomposition)
Formal grammars ↔ graph decomposition (rooted grammar producing subcubic outerplanar graphs from branches and path fragments)
Computer-verified certificate checking ↔ combinatorial existence proofs (finite certificate closure verified by a stand-alone checker)

      -- Red vertices have minimum degree at least 1 in the red-induced subgraph

directions.proof_strategy: First formalize subcubic outerplanar graphs and the crumby coloring property. Then formalize the rooted grammatical decomposition: every finite simple subcubic outerplanar graph decomposes recursively via rooted branches and two-terminal path fragments, with cyclic blocks handled by deleting the root. Define crumby-admissible colorings that allow temporary isolated red vertices at boundary locations (the root of a rooted branch, or the two terminals of a path fragment). Prove by induction on the grammar that every decomposed graph admits a crumby-admissible coloring, reducing to verifying an explicit finite family of lower certificates (boundary types and root states). The finite verification that the certificate family is closed under all decomposition steps and that every completed branch contains a final-legal root state can be automated via decidable computation, while the structural reductions and certificate-induction principle are proved by hand.
directions.title: Every subcubic outerplanar graph admits a crumby coloring

directions.description: The paper proves that for any fixed c ∈ [1, √2), there exist finite metric spaces requiring exponentially large finitely presented c-approximations of the Vietoris-Rips filtration, and that for any c ≥ 1, superlinear size is necessary. This conjecture posits that √2 is the sharp threshold between exponential and polynomial approximability: for every fixed c ≥ √2, there exists a polynomial p_c such that every finite metric space X admits a finitely presented c-approximation to VR(X) of size at most p_c(|X|). This would yield a complete dichotomy—exponential below √2, polynomial at or above √2—matching the natural geometric breakpoint where the Rips complex becomes the full simplex on any metric space with all distances ≤ 2r.
domain_bridges: computational complexity theory (threshold phenomena in approximability)

    ∃ (F : Filtration ℝ SimplicialComplex) (hF_fp : FinitelyPresented F)

The key insight should be that at approximation factor √2, the homotopy interleaving relaxation is strong enough to allow collapse of high-dimensional simplices that are forced in the exact filtration. A potential approach: (1) Show that for c ≥ √2, any finite metric space can be embedded into a space of bounded doubling dimension with distortion at most √2, then invoke Sheehy-type sparse approximation results; (2) Alternatively, directly construct a filtration that is homotopy-interleaved with VR(X) at factor √2 using controlled local collapses whose combinatorial complexity is polynomially bounded.
directions.title: The √2-Threshold Conjecture for Rips Filtration Approximation

directions.description: A meme is a unit of cultural information that replicates through human minds. Model meme propagation as a sheaf over the social network graph: each node is a person, each edge is a communication channel, and the meme is a section of the sheaf that must satisfy consistency conditions at each node. Define meme fitness as the sheaf cohomology group H^1(G, M) where G is the social network and M is the meme sheaf. A meme with H^1 = 0 is universally transmissible (it has no consistency barriers — anyone can understand it). A meme with H^1 of dimension d requires d 'interpretation steps' to cross between communities. Conjecture: The most viral memes have H^1(G, M) = 0 but H^0(G, M) of maximal dimension — they spread everywhere AND mean different things to different communities. The dimension of H^0 counts the number of distinct interpretations. A meme that means the same thing to everyone has dim(H^0) = 1 and dim(H^1) = 0. A meme that means different things to different communities has dim(H^0) > 1 and dim(H^1) = 0. A meme that CANNOT spread between communities has H^1 > 0. Test: model Twitter/X retweet networks as graphs G with 1000 nodes, assign meme sheaves based on community structure, compute H^0 and H^1, and correlate with actual virality data. Impact: meme virality is a topological property — it's not about content quality but about the sheaf cohomology of the social network.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the meme sheaf M on social network G: for each community C_i (cluster in G), M(C_i) is the set of interpretations of the meme in community i. For each edge between communities, there is a restriction map M(C_i) -> M(C_j) that transforms the meme's meaning. Define H^0(G, M) = kernel of the coboundary map (interpretations that are consistent across ALL communities). Define H^1(G, M) = cokernel (obstructions to consistent interpretation). Prove: dim(H^0) = number of universal interpretations. Prove: dim(H^1) = number of community-pairs where the meme CANNOT be consistently transmitted. Virality = dim(H^0) / (dim(H^0) + dim(H^1)) — the fraction of interpretations that spread without obstruction. Test: for 3 communities with sheaf values M(C1) = R, M(C2) = R, M(C3) = R^2 and restriction maps that mix coordinates, compute H^0 and H^1 and verify that high virality memes have H^1 = 0 and dim(H^0) > 1.
directions.title: The Mathematics of Memes: Viral Information Topology

directions.description: Euclid's parallel postulate says parallel lines never meet. Hyperbolic geometry says they can diverge. Elliptic geometry says they converge. But what about a geometry where parallel lines BOTH converge AND diverge? Define a Split Geometry on R^2 where the parallel postulate is direction-dependent: lines parallel to the x-axis diverge (hyperbolic behavior) while lines parallel to the y-axis converge (elliptic behavior). The metric is ds^2 = dx^2/cosh^2(y) + dy^2 * cosh^2(x) — expanding in x and contracting in y. Conjecture: Split Geometry is a consistent Riemannian geometry with curvature K(x,y) = -sech^2(y) + sech^2(x) that changes sign across the diagonals. The geometry has a 'phase boundary' along the lines y = x and y = -x where K = 0 (flat). In the region |x| > |y|, K > 0 (elliptic) and in the region |y| > |x|, K < 0 (hyperbolic). The geodesics in split geometry are piecewise combinations of exponential curves (in hyperbolic regions) and trigonometric curves (in elliptic regions). Test: compute the Christoffel symbols and curvature tensor for the split metric. Prove that geodesics cross the phase boundary at most twice. Compute the area of a split triangle with one vertex in each region. Impact: a geometry where the curvature of space depends on which direction you look — the mathematical realization of a universe that is simultaneously expanding and contracting.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the split metric g = diag(1/cosh^2(y), cosh^2(x)) on R^2. Compute the Christoffel symbols: Gamma^1_{11} = tanh(y), Gamma^1_{12} = 0, Gamma^1_{22} = -sinh(x)cosh(x), Gamma^2_{11} = -tanh(y)*cosh^2(x)*cosh^2(y), Gamma^2_{12} = 0, Gamma^2_{22} = -sinh(x)cosh(x). Compute curvature: K = -sech^2(y) + sech^2(x). Verify: K = 0 on y = x and y = -x. K > 0 for |x| > |y| (elliptic). K < 0 for |y| > |x| (hyperbolic). Prove geodesic crossing: a geodesic that enters the elliptic region and then the hyperbolic region crosses the flat boundary at most twice (by convexity of the curvature sign along the geodesic). Compute split triangle area: integral of sqrt(det(g)) = integral of cosh(x)/cosh(y) over the triangle. Test: numerical verification for specific triangles.
directions.title: Impossible Geometries: Where Parallel Lines Converge AND Diverge

directions.description: Proofs are static objects, but what if proofs could improve? Define a proof refinement system where each proof P has a complexity C(P) = length(P) + depth(P) + number of lemmas, and a proof P' is a refinement of P if P' proves the same theorem with C(P') < C(P). Conjecture: For every theorem T provable in ZFC, there exists a sequence of refinements P = P_0, P_1, P_2, ... such that C(P_n) is non-increasing and the limit P_infinity is the simplest proof of T (in the sense of Kolmogorov complexity). Moreover, the refinement process halts: there exists N such that C(P_N) = C(P_{N+1}) = ... = C(P_infinity). The key insight: proof simplification is a well-founded process because the complexity is a natural number that decreases at each step. But the process can be arbitrarily long — the proof of the four-color theorem might require 10^100 refinements to reach its simplest form. Test: formalize the refinement system in Lean 4. Starting from the statement of the irrationality of sqrt(2), generate refinements by eliminating unnecessary lemmas, shortening case splits, and removing redundant quantifiers. Measure C(P) at each step and verify it decreases. Impact: proofs are not static — they are living objects that can be improved. The simplest proof of a theorem is the LIMIT of the refinement process, and this limit ALWAYS exists.
directions.proof_strategy: Define proof complexity C(P) = length(P) + depth(P) + number_of_lemmas(P) for a proof P in a formal system. Define refinement: P' refines P if P' proves the same theorem as P and C(P') < C(P). Prove: the refinement process is well-founded — there is no infinite decreasing chain C(P_0) > C(P_1) > ... because C takes values in the natural numbers. Prove: the limit P_infinity exists because the chain must terminate at a proof of minimal complexity. Prove the refinement process can be arbitrarily long: construct a theorem T such that the simplest proof of T has complexity C_min, but the initial proof has complexity C_max, and C_max - C_min can be made arbitrarily large. Example: the proof of 'there exist n consecutive composite numbers' requires induction up to n, but the simplest proof uses only the factorial n! + 2, n! + 3, ..., n! + n. Test: implement refinement for sqrt(2) irrationality in Lean 4.
directions.title: Self-Improving Proofs: Proofs That Get Simpler Over Time

directions.description: L-functions are the DNA of mathematics — each one encodes deep arithmetic information. But how many L-functions ARE there? The L-function universe is vast: (1) The Riemann zeta function (1 L-function), (2) Dirichlet L-functions (countably many), (3) L-functions of elliptic curves (uncountably many, one per j-invariant), (4) L-functions of modular forms (countably many, but indexed by weight and level), (5) L-functions of Galois representations (enormous family). Conjecture: The set of 'natural' L-functions (those satisfying the Selberg class axioms: analytic continuation, functional equation, Euler product, Ramanujan bound) is COUNTABLE. This means the universe of well-behaved L-functions is no bigger than the integers, despite each individual L-function encoding infinitely much information. The Selberg class is a universe of countable stars, each one an entire galaxy. Test: prove that the Selberg class is countable by showing that each L-function is determined by a finite set of data (degree, conductor, root number, Euler factors at finitely many primes). Enumerate the first 100 elements of the Selberg class ordered by conductor. Impact: the mathematical universe of L-functions is countable — there are only as many well-behaved L-functions as integers. Each one contains infinite depth, but there are only countably many of them.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the Selberg class S as the set of Dirichlet series L(s) = sum a_n/n^s satisfying: (1) Ramanujan bound |a_n| <= n^epsilon for epsilon > 0, (2) Analytic continuation to C except for a possible pole at s=1, (3) Functional equation relating L(s) to L(1-s), (4) Euler product L(s) = prod_p L_p(s). Prove S is countable: each L in S is determined by finitely many data because (a) the degree d_L is a positive integer, (b) the conductor q_L is a positive integer, (c) the Euler factors L_p(s) for p not dividing q_L are determined by the Ramanujan bound and the functional equation, and (d) there are finitely many primes dividing q_L. So L is determined by (d_L, q_L, epsilon_L, {L_p(s) : p | q_L}), a finite set of data. Since each piece of data is countable, S is countable. Test: enumerate elements of S by increasing conductor.
directions.title: The L-Function Universe: A Cosmic Census of All L-Functions

directions.description: Godel's incompleteness theorem says there are true statements that cannot be proved. But what if we turn incompleteness into a GAME? Define Godel's Casino: a game where the player bets on the truth value of statements that are independent of ZFC. The house deals cards representing arithmetic statements, and the player must bet TRUE or FALSE. The Continuum Hypothesis is the first card — you can bet either way and you're RIGHT in some model. Conjecture: Godel's Casino has a winning strategy that guarantees expected profit > 0, even though individual bets are undecidable. The strategy: bet TRUE on Sigma_1 statements (they're true if provable, and ZFC is Sigma_1-complete), bet FALSE on Pi_1 statements that are known to be independent (like Con(ZFC)), and bet on the CONSERVATIVE extension for statements that are genuinely undecidable. The expected profit per round is at least 1/3 because at least 1/3 of arithmetic statements are decidable (by the arithmetic hierarchy: the fraction of statements at level n that are decidable at level n is at least 1/3). Test: simulate Godel's Casino with 1000 independent ZFC statements and verify the winning strategy achieves expected profit > 0. Impact: incompleteness is not a barrier — it's an opportunity. You can WIN at the game of undecidability.
directions.proof_strategy: Define Godel's Casino: each round, the house presents a statement phi in the language of arithmetic. The player bets TRUE or FALSE. If ZFC proves phi, TRUE wins. If ZFC proves not-phi, FALSE wins. If phi is independent of ZFC, BOTH bets win (the player gets their stake back plus a bonus). Strategy: bet TRUE on Sigma_1 statements, FALSE on negations of Con(ZFC) and similar independent Pi_1 statements. Prove expected profit > 0: by the arithmetic hierarchy, Sigma_1 statements are decidable (true iff provable). For a random statement at level n, the probability of decidability is at least 1/3 (by counting). So E[profit] >= (1/3) * (stake) > 0. The key: even though individual bets are undecidable, the AGGREGATE strategy is profitable because most arithmetic statements ARE decidable. Test: simulate with 1000 randomly generated arithmetic statements at various levels of the hierarchy.
directions.title: Godel's Casino: Incomplete but Winnable Games

directions.description: We conjecture that for any integers r > s ≥ 3, the minimal possible K_r-density among graphons with prescribed K_s-density λ is given by the classical multipartite edge-to-clique profile re‑parametrised by λ, and that the stability theorem holds for the whole range of λ (including the endpoint λ = 0). In particular, there exists a quantitative function φ such that if a graphon W satisfies K_s(W) = λ and K_r(W) ≤ f_{r,s}(λ) + ε, then the cut distance from W to the extremal multipartite family determined by λ is bounded by φ(ε).

  let f := multipartite_profile r s lambda;  -- placeholder for the reparametrised profile
  ∃ (F : extremal_family r s lambda), 
    ∀ (W : Graphon), (hKs : K_s W = lambda), (hKr : K_r W ≤ f + epsilon) → 
      delta_cut W F ≤ phi epsilon := by
  -- proof skeleton
  have hpos : 0 ≤ lambda ∧∧ lambda ≤ lambda_max from …
  -- case lambda > 0: apply existing stability theorem
  -- case lambda = 0: prove trivial stability using density‑cut norm inequality
  -- combine via cases
directions.proof_strategy: Build on the existing proof of the higher‑order clique density theorem to extend the analysis to the zero‑density endpoint. Use the existing stability argument for the positive branch, which relies on the first variation formula and the classification of extremal graphons. To handle the λ = 0 case, one must show that the only extremal graphons are those with vanishing edge density, i.e., the empty graph, and that any near‑extremal graphon must be close (in cut distance) to the empty graph. This requires a new quantitative inequality for the K_s-density in terms of the cut norm of the graphon, derivable from the moment method and the known lower bound for the K_r-density. The resulting φ(ε) can be taken linear in ε. Formalizing the conjecture in Lean will involve defining graphons as measurable functions on a probability space, the K_t-density functional, and cut distance, then encoding the inequalities as lemmas that can be proved by induction on r-s.
directions.title: Higher-order clique density stability conjecture

directions.description:
For each fixed interval length \(y\in\mathbb{N}\), define \(W(x,y)=\sum_{j=1}^{y}\omega(x+j)\) where \(\omega(n)\) counts distinct prime factors of \(n\). The conjecture states that the growth of \(W\) is sharply bounded: 
\[ \limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{W(x,y)\log\log x}{\log x}=1.\]
This captures the maximal possible order of the sum of distinct prime factors in a block of \(y\) consecutive integers.

directions.proof_strategy: The conjecture is motivated by a refined abc‑type conjecture involving the kernel function \(H(n)=\gamma(n)/(\log\gamma(n))^{\omega(n)}\). Using heuristic arguments from the abc conjecture, sieve methods, and extreme‑value theory for additive functions, one can show that the upper bound \((\log x)/\log\log x\) is best possible and that the limsup equals 1. In a formal development, the plan is to (i) define \(\omega\) and \(W\) in Lean, (ii) prove elementary bounds (e.g., \(\omega(n)\le \log n/\log\log n\)), (iii) encode the limsup condition via a universal quantifier over \(\varepsilon>0\) and an existence statement for infinitely many \(x\), and (iv) attempt a contradiction proof assuming a larger limsup.
directions.title: Precise asymptotic for the sum of distinct prime divisors over intervals

In other words, there exists a constant \(C assemblies(r,\Sigma)\in\Q^\times\) such that
\[
\langle Z_{\pi}^{r},Z_{\pi}^{r}\rangle
= C\bigl(r,\Sigma\bigr)\cdot L_{F'/F}^{(r)}(\pi,\tfrac12).\n\]
The conjecture is formulated for all integers \(r\ge 1\) and all finite – but not necessarily square‑free – divisors \(\Sigma\).

directions.description:
We conjecture that the combinatorial condition defining reflected bounded‑growth tuples can be expressed solely by simple linear inequalities and parity constraints on a weakly increasing integer sequence.  In other words, for a tuple \(a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in\mathbb{N}^n\) the following are equivalent:

1. \(a\) is a reflected bounded‑growth tuple (as defined in the paper).
2. \(a\) is weakly increasing, satisfies \(a_i\le 2i-1\) for all \(i\), and has parity condition \(a_i\equiv i-1\pmod 2\) whenever \(i\) is odd.

Consequently the map \(a\mapsto\prod_{i=1}^n[ a_i+1 ]_q\) gives a bijection between such tuples and the palindromic Poincaré polynomials of type \(B_n\) which do not lie in the image of Stembridge's bottom map from type \(A_{n+1}\).  This yields a purely elementary description of the complete list of palindromic Poincaré polynomials in type \(B\).
directions.lean_theorem_stub:
-- Characterisation of reflected bounded‑growth tuples

theorem reflected_bounded_growth_iff :
  ∀ {n : ℕ} (a : Vector ℕ n),
    is_reflected_bounded_growth a ↔
      (monotone a ∧
       ∀ i : Fin n, a i ≤ 2 * (i + 1) - 1 ∧
         ((i + 1) % 2 = 1 → a i % 2 = i % 2)) := by
  -- The proof is split into two directions:
  -- • (→) Assume \`a\` is a reflected bounded‑growth tuple.
  --   By definition there is a weakly increasing sequence \`b\` with \`b_i ≤ 2i-1\` and parity property;
  --   the reflection argument yields the stated inequalities for \`a\`.
  -- • (←) Assume the linear/parity conditions.
  --   Construct a weakly increasing sequence \`b\` by setting \`b_i = a_{n-i+1}\` and verify that \`b\`
  --   satisfies the required bounds, thereby producing a reflected bounded‑growth tuple whose image is \`a\`.
  -- The details are handled by elementary arithmetic lemmas in Lean.
directions.proof_strategy:
We will formalise the conjecture in Lean 4 by defining the predicate \`is_reflected_bounded_growth\` on vectors of natural numbers, the monotonicity and inequality/parity conditions, and the associated product of \(q\)-integers.  The plan is:

1. Implement the definitions in Lean.
2. Compute the set of tuples satisfying the linear/parity characterisation for small ranks (e.g., \(n\le 8\)) and compare with the known list of reflected bounded‑growth tuples extracted from the paper (via brute‑force enumeration).
3. Use the verification for small \(n\) to gain confidence, then attempt an inductive proof that exploits the recursive structure of \(B_n\) and the relationship with the bottom map from \(A_{n+1}\).

The final theorem will assert the equivalence described above.
directions.title: Characterizing reflected bounded‑growth tuples in type B

directions.description: The field with one element F_1 is a hypothetical object that would explain why the Weil conjectures have the form they do — as if there were a field with q^0 = 1 element. Tropical geometry replaces addition with min and multiplication with addition. What if these two ideas are the SAME? Conjecture: The tropical semiring (R union {infinity}, min, +) IS the field with one element, in the following precise sense: the category of tropical schemes is equivalent to the category of F_1-schemes. More concretely, a tropical variety over F_1 is a set with a min-plus structure, and its base change to Z (formally, tensor with Z) is a toric variety. The key correspondence: F_1-points of a tropical variety are the vertices of its Newton polytope, and the 'cardinality' of the tropical variety (as an F_1-object) is the number of lattice points in the polytope, which equals the degree of the toric variety after base change. Test: for each toric variety corresponding to a polytope P, compute the number of F_1-points (vertices of P) and verify that the Euler characteristic of the toric variety equals |vertices(P)| = #F_1-points. Prove the tensor product correspondence: tropical scheme X over F_1 has X tensor_Z Z = the corresponding toric variety. Impact: F_1 and tropical geometry are two faces of the same coin. The field with one element is tropical, and tropical geometry is the geometry of F_1.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the F_1-tropical correspondence: a tropical scheme over F_1 is a monoid object M in the tropical semiring (R union infty, min, +). The base change M tensor_Z Z is the monoid algebra Z[M], which is the coordinate ring of the toric variety associated to M. Prove: if M is the monoid of lattice points in a rational polytope P, then Z[M] is the homogeneous coordinate ring of the toric variety V(P). Prove the point-counting correspondence: #V(P)(F_1) = |vertices(P)| (number of F_1-points equals vertices). Prove: chi(V(P)) = |vertices(P)| (Euler characteristic equals number of F_1-points). This follows from the fact that V(P) is a cell complex with one cell per face of P, and chi = alternating sum of face counts = number of vertices. Test: verify for projective space P^n (the simplex has n+1 vertices, chi(P^n) = n+1), for the Hirzebruch surface F_a (4 vertices, chi = 4).
directions.title: Tropical Dreams: The Field with One Element Meets Tropical Geometry

directions.description: Prime gaps — the spaces between consecutive primes — are like empty cells in a crossword puzzle. The gaps are 1, 2, 2, 4, 2, 4, 2, 4, 6, 2, 6, 4, 2, 4, 6, 6, 2, 6, 4, 2, ... (OEIS A001223). The pattern seems random, but the crossword has rules: (1) All prime gaps are even (except the first gap of 1 between 2 and 3). (2) A gap g can only appear at position n if n+g is prime and all of n+1, n+2, ..., n+g-1 are composite. (3) The density of gap g near n is approximately 2*C_2/(g*log(n)) where C_2 is the twin prime constant. Conjecture: The prime gap crossword is uniquely solvable — given the pattern of gaps up to N, the next prime is determined with probability 1 - O(1/log(N)). More precisely, the conditional probability that the next prime after p is p + g, given all primes up to p, is approximately 2*C_2/g * (1/log(p)) * product_{q prime, q | g} (q-1)/(q-2). This is the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture for prime gaps. But the crossword has a surprise: certain gap patterns FORCE the next number. For example, if the gaps near n are 6, 4, 2, 6, then the next gap is almost certainly 4 (the only way to fill the crossword). Test: compute the conditional probabilities for prime gaps up to 10^8 and verify they match the Hardy-Littlewood prediction. Find forcing patterns (gaps that uniquely determine the next prime) and prove they occur with positive density. Impact: prime gaps are not random — they are a solvable crossword puzzle with deterministic rules.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the prime gap sequence g(n) = p(n+1) - p(n) for n >= 1. State the Hardy-Littlewood gap conjecture: P(g(n) = g | g(n-1) = g_{-1}, ...) = 2*C_2/g * (1/log(p(n))) * product_{q prime, q | g} (q-1)/(q-2) where C_2 = 0.66016... is the twin prime constant. Define forcing patterns: a sequence of gaps g_{-k}, ..., g_{-1} is forcing if P(g(0) = g | g_{-k}, ..., g_{-1}) > 0.99 for exactly one value of g. Prove forcing patterns have positive density: the pattern [6, 4, 2, 6] is forcing because after primes p, p+6, p+10, p+12, p+18, the next prime must be p+22 with probability > 0.95 (since p+20 is even, p+21 is divisible by 3 if p ≡ 1 mod 3, etc.). Compute conditional probabilities numerically for N = 10^8. Test: enumerate forcing patterns and compute their density.
directions.title: The Prime Number Crossword: Filling the Gaps in the Primes

directions.description: Hilbert's Hotel has infinitely many rooms, each containing a prime number. Room n contains the n-th prime p_n. The manager can always accommodate a new guest (there are infinitely many primes). But what if the guests want to REARRANGE? Conjecture: For any permutation sigma of N, there exists a rearrangement of the primes q_1, q_2, ... such that the sequence of ratios q_n / p_n converges to 1. In other words, you can shuffle the primes almost arbitrarily and the room numbers barely change. More precisely, the set of permutations sigma for which p_{sigma(n)} / p_n has a limit is dense in the symmetric group (with the topology of pointwise convergence). But NOT every permutation works: the permutation that swaps all even-indexed primes with odd-indexed ones gives q_{2n}/p_{2n} = p_{2n-1}/p_{2n} which converges to 1 by the prime number theorem, but the permutation that reverses order gives q_n/p_n = p_{N-n}/p_n which diverges. Test: compute q_n/p_n for 10 random permutations of the first 10^6 primes and verify that most ratios converge to 1. Find the exact density of 'well-behaved' permutations. Impact: the primes are robust under rearrangement — their asymptotic density is a topological invariant of the permutation group.
directions.proof_strategy: Define a rearrangement of primes as a bijection sigma: N -> N, giving q_n = p_{sigma(n)}. Define a well-behaved rearrangement as one where q_n/p_n -> 1. Prove density: for any epsilon > 0 and any finite partial permutation sigma_0, there exists an extension sigma such that q_n/p_n -> 1. Use the prime number theorem: p_n ~ n*log(n), so q_n/p_n = p_{sigma(n)}/(n*log(n)) = sigma(n)*log(sigma(n))/(n*log(n)). For this to converge to 1, we need sigma(n) ~ n, i.e., sigma must be 'close to the identity' in the sense that sigma(n)/n -> 1. Prove the set of such permutations is dense in Sym(N): for any finite permutation and any neighborhood, extend to a permutation with sigma(n) = n + O(sqrt(n)*log(n)) which satisfies sigma(n)/n -> 1. Prove the reversal fails: sigma(n) = N-n gives sigma(n)/n = (N-n)/n -> infinity. Test: sample 1000 permutations from Sym(10^6) and measure the fraction that are well-behaved.
directions.title: Hilbert's Hotel for Primes: An Infinite Hotel Where Every Guest Is Prime

directions.description: The Mandelbrot set M is defined by z_{n+1} = z_n^2 + c, and the boundary of M is the locus of c values where the orbit of 0 is bounded but barely so. Each bulb of M corresponds to a rational number p/q (the period-q bulb at angle p/q). The size of the p/q bulb decreases with q, and the Fibonacci sequence governs the spiral arrangement of bulbs. Conjecture: The period of the bulb at angle p/q (in lowest terms) is exactly q. Moreover, the Lyapunov exponent lambda(c) at the center of the p/q bulb equals log(2) * cos(pi*p/q). The 'prime bulbs' — bulbs at angles 1/q where q is prime — have special symmetry: they are the only bulbs with dihedral symmetry D_q. The composite bulbs have more complex symmetry groups. The prime factorization of the period determines the bulb's topology: a bulb of period n = p1^a1 * ... * pk^ak is topologically a product of k bulbs of periods p1^a1, ..., pk^ak. Test: for each rational p/q with q <= 20, locate the corresponding bulb in M, compute its Lyapunov exponent, and verify lambda = log(2) * cos(pi*p/q). Classify bulbs by the prime factorization of their period and verify the product structure. Impact: the Mandelbrot set is a visual calculator for prime factorization — every bulb encodes number-theoretic information about its period.
directions.proof_strategy: State the bulb-period correspondence: the bulb at angle p/q in the Mandelbrot set has period q. This follows from the Douady-Hubbard landing theorem. Conjecture the Lyapunov formula: lambda(center of p/q bulb) = log(2) * cos(pi*p/q). Prove for the main cardioid (period 1): lambda = log(2) * cos(0) = log(2). Prove for the period-2 bulb: lambda = log(2) * cos(pi/2) = 0 (parabolic). Prove for period-q bulbs: the critical orbit has period q, and the multiplier of the q-cycle equals e^{2*pi*i*p/q} at the center, so the Lyapunov exponent is log|multiplier| = log(2) * cos(2*pi*p/q). Wait, the multiplier at the center of the p/q bulb is e^{2*pi*i*p/q}, so |multiplier| = 1 and lambda = 0. The Lyapunov exponent is NOT log(2)*cos(pi*p/q) at the center. Correct: on the boundary of the p/q bulb, lambda = 0 (parabolic), and lambda increases as you move away. Test: compute lambda numerically along rays from bulb centers.
directions.title: The Mandelbrot Set's Secret Number Theory: Quadratic Recurrence and Primality

directions.description: When a theorem prover searches for a proof, it explores a tree of possible derivation steps. The branching factor is the number of applicable inference rules at each step. Define the proof-search fractal dimension D(T) of a theorem T as the Hausdorff dimension of the set of all successful proof paths for T. If D(T) < 1, the proof is 'easy' (few paths work, so search is focused). If D(T) > 1, the proof is 'hard' (many paths must be explored). Conjecture: For theorems in ZFC, D(T) = 1 + O(1/length(T)). In other words, most theorems have fractal dimension close to 1 — proof search is neither trivially easy nor impossibly hard, but balanced at the edge. Theorems with D(T) << 1 are 'obvious' (direct proofs), and theorems with D(T) >> 1 require exponentially long proofs. The fractal dimension correlates with proof length: if D(T) = 1 + epsilon, then the shortest proof of T has length roughly 1/epsilon. Test: for 1000 theorems in Lean 4's Mathlib, estimate D(T) by Monte Carlo sampling of proof search trees, and correlate with actual proof length. Impact: proof difficulty is a fractal — the dimension of the proof search space determines how hard the theorem is.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the proof search tree for a theorem T: nodes are proof states, edges are inference rule applications, and leaves are states where T is proved or a contradiction is reached. Define the successful path set S(T) as the set of all paths from root to a successful leaf. Define D(T) = dim_H(S(T)) as the Hausdorff dimension. Compute D(T) by box-counting: cover S(T) with boxes of size epsilon and count N(epsilon) boxes. Then D(T) = lim_{epsilon -> 0} log(N(epsilon))/log(1/epsilon). For a balanced binary tree of depth d with 2^d leaves, D = log(2)/log(2) = 1. For a sparse tree with branching factor b < 2, D = log(b)/log(2) < 1. Conjecture: for typical ZFC theorems, the effective branching factor approaches 2 from below, giving D -> 1. Estimate D(T) by MCMC: start from the goal state, randomly apply inference rules, and count the fraction of paths that reach axioms within depth d. D(T) = log(fraction * branching_factor) / log(2). Test: compute for 1000 Mathlib theorems.
directions.title: Fractal Dimension of Proof Search: How Hard Is It to Find a Proof?

directions.description: Elementary cellular automata (ECAs) are the 256 rules that update a 1D binary array based on its 3-cell neighborhood. Rule 110 is Turing-complete. But ECAs can also be viewed as polynomial maps over GF(2): the state s = (s_0, s_1, ..., s_{n-1}) is a vector over GF(2), and the update rule is s -> f(s) where f is a degree-3 polynomial (since the rule depends on 3 cells). Conjecture: The algebraic variety V(f) = {s : f(s) = s} (fixed points of the ECA) has dimension equal to the 'complexity class' of the rule. For simple rules (e.g., Rule 0, which is all zeros), V(f) has dimension 0 (a single point). For complex rules (e.g., Rule 110), V(f) has maximal dimension. The Grothendieck-style approach: each ECA defines a sheaf on the state space, and the global sections of this sheaf classify the possible stable configurations. Rule 110's sheaf has the richest section structure, corresponding to its Turing-completeness. Test: compute dim(V(f)) for all 256 ECAs and verify that the dimension correlates with Wolfram's complexity classification (Class 1: dim=0, Class 2: dim<=n/2, Class 3: dim>=n/2, Class 4: dim=n). Impact: cellular automata are algebraic varieties, and their complexity is the dimension of their fixed-point variety.
directions.proof_strategy: Encode ECA state as vector s in GF(2)^n. Rule r defines update f_r(s)_i = g(s_{i-1}, s_i, s_{i+1}) where g is the truth table of rule r, viewed as a polynomial over GF(2). For example, Rule 110: g(a,b,c) = a + b + ac + bc (mod 2). Fixed points satisfy f_r(s) = s, a system of n polynomial equations over GF(2). Compute dim(V(f_r)) using Groebner basis methods. For Rule 0: f_0(s) = 0, so V = {0}, dim = 0. For Rule 255: f_255(s) = 1+s, V = {1+s = s} = {1=0} = empty, dim = -1 (no fixed points). For Rule 110: f_110(s) = s + s_{i-1} + s_i + s_{i-1}*s_{i+1} + s_i*s_{i+1}, dim(V) = n - rank(Jacobian of f-s). Conjecture: dim(V(f_r)) correlates with Wolfram class. Test: compute dim(V(f_r)) for all 256 rules with n=20 and compare to Wolfram classification.
directions.title: Cellular Automata as Algebraic Geometry: Wolfram's Rules Meet Grothendieck

directions.description: Every recipe is an algorithm: it takes ingredients (inputs) and produces a dish (output). The question is: can you verify a good dish faster than you can cook it? This is exactly P vs NP, but in the kitchen. Define the verification time V(R) of a recipe R as the time it takes to taste the dish and determine if it's good. Define the cooking time C(R) as the time it takes to prepare the dish. Conjecture: For most traditional recipes, C(R) > V(R) — cooking takes longer than tasting (P != NP in the kitchen). But there exist 'quick recipes' where C(R) = V(R) — assemble-and-serve dishes like salads (P = NP in the kitchen). The interesting class is 'NP-hard recipes' — dishes where even VERifying the result is hard. Example: is the souffle risen? You can only verify by cutting it open, which destroys it. Theorem: souffle verification is co-NP-hard because determining if a souffle will rise requires simulating the thermodynamic process, which is PSPACE-hard. More formally: the souffle function S(ingredients, temperature, time) -> {risen, collapsed} requires computing the Navier-Stokes equations for the batter, which is PSPACE-hard. Test: classify 100 recipes by their C(R)/V(R) ratio. Verify that P = NP recipes have C = V, while P != NP recipes have C >> V. Impact: computational complexity is not abstract — it shows up in your kitchen. Some dishes are inherently harder to make than to verify.
directions.proof_strategy: Define kitchen complexity: a recipe R is a tuple (ingredients, operations, output). Verification time V(R) = time to determine output quality (tasting). Cooking time C(R) = time to execute operations. Define Kitchen-P = {R : C(R) = O(poly(|R|))} — recipes that can be cooked in polynomial time. Define Kitchen-NP = {R : V(R) = O(poly(|R|))} — recipes that can be verified in polynomial time. Prove: salad is in Kitchen-P (chop and mix, linear time). Prove: souffle is Kitchen-NP-hard: verifying a souffle's rise requires computing the Navier-Stokes dynamics of the batter, which is PSPACE-hard. Prove Kitchen-P != Kitchen-NP for souffles: the Navier-Stokes computation cannot be shortcut. Classify 100 recipes: P=P (salads, sandwiches, smoothies), P<NP (baked goods, braises, ferments), P<<NP (souffles, tempered chocolate, molecular gastronomy). Test: time 50 people making 10 recipes each, measure cooking time vs verification time.
directions.title: The P vs NP of Cooking: Computational Complexity of Recipes

directions.description: Two quantum particles are entangled if measuring one instantly affects the other. But entanglement is also a topological property: if you represent the state of two qubits as a curve in R^3, entanglement IS the linking number. Conjecture: For any pure state of two qubits |psi> in C^2 tensor C^2, the concurrence C(psi) = 2|alpha*delta - beta*gamma| (where psi = alpha|00> + beta|01> + gamma|10> + delta|11>) equals the absolute value of the linking number of two curves derived from the Hopf fibration applied to psi. Specifically, map psi to S^7 via normalization, then project to S^4 via the Hopf map, and the preimages of two points in S^4 are linked circles in S^7 whose linking number equals the concurrence. This means: entanglement is MEASURED by topology, and maximally entangled states correspond to the Hopf link (linking number 1). Test: for 1000 random two-qubit states, compute the concurrence and the linking number of the Hopf preimages, and verify they are equal. Prove the equality for the Bell states. Impact: quantum entanglement is not mysterious — it is the linking number of the Hopf fibration. Two particles are entangled if and only if their Hopf preimages are linked.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the Hopf fibration: S^3 -> S^2 by (z1, z2) -> (2*z1*z2_bar, |z1|^2 - |z2|^2). For a two-qubit state psi = alpha|00> + beta|01> + gamma|10> + delta|11>, define the reduced state rho_1 = Tr_2(|psi><psi|). The concurrence is C = 2|alpha*delta - beta*gamma|. Map: given psi, form the complex matrix M = [[alpha, beta], [gamma, delta]]. The concurrence equals 2|det(M)| = 2|alpha*delta - beta*gamma|. Now the Hopf linking: consider the curves gamma_1(t) = (alpha*e^{it}, beta) / ||(alpha*e^{it}, beta)|| and gamma_2(t) = (gamma*e^{it}, delta) / ||(gamma*e^{it}, delta)|| in S^3. The linking number of gamma_1 and gamma_2 in S^3 equals |det(M)| (by the Whitehead formula for linking in S^3). Therefore C = 2 * |linking number|. Normalizing: C/2 = |linking number|, so the normalized concurrence equals the linking number. For Bell states: |Phi+> = (|00>+|11>)/sqrt(2) has alpha=delta=1/sqrt(2), beta=gamma=0, C=1, linking number=1. For product states: |00> has C=0, linking number=0. Test: verify for 1000 random states.
directions.title: Quantum Entanglement as Algebraic Topology: The Linking Number Is Entanglement

directions.description: Mendeleev's periodic table arranges elements by atomic number Z, but Z is just the charge of the nucleus. Conjecture: the periodic table is the spectrum of an operator on a Hilbert space of dimension equal to the number of stable isotopes. Define the 'nuclear Hamiltonian' H on L^2(R^3) by H = -hbar^2/(2m) * nabla^2 + V(r) where V(r) encodes the strong and electromagnetic forces. The eigenvalues E_n of H give the binding energies of nuclei, and Z_n = round(E_n / E_0) gives the atomic numbers. The 'periodicity' of the table arises because the eigenvalues of H have shell structure (like the hydrogen atom): the n-th shell has degeneracy 2n^2 (from the angular momentum quantum number), giving shell sizes 2, 8, 18, 32, 50, 72 — the noble gas atomic numbers 2, 10, 28, 60, 110 are the cumulative sums. The 'stability islands' (magic numbers 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126) correspond to extra degeneracies in the nuclear potential. Test: solve the Schrodinger equation for a Woods-Saxon potential (model nuclear potential) and show that the eigenvalue degeneracies match the periodic table structure. Compute the 'predicted' periodic table from the eigenvalues and compare with reality. Impact: chemistry IS applied spectral theory. The periodic table is the spectrum of a Hamiltonian, and every chemical property is an eigenvalue.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the nuclear Hamiltonian H = -hbar^2/(2m) * nabla^2 + V(r) where V(r) = -V_0 / (1 + exp((r-R)/a)) (Woods-Saxon potential). Solve the radial Schrodinger equation for H in spherical coordinates. The eigenvalues E_{n,l} have degeneracy 2(2l+1) (spin-orbit coupling doubles the angular momentum degeneracy). The magic numbers arise when a shell is completely filled: cumulative degeneracies give 2, 6+2=8, 6+2+10+2=20, etc. (with spin-orbit splitting). Compute: solve the Schrodinger equation numerically for V_0 = 50 MeV, R = 1.2*A^{1/3} fm, a = 0.5 fm. Extract eigenvalues and compare with observed nuclear binding energies. The key insight: spin-orbit coupling (V_{ls} = V_{ls0} * (1/r) * dV/dr * L dot S) splits the (n,l) levels into (n,l,j=l+1/2) and (n,l,j=l-1/2), creating the magic numbers 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126. Test: compute eigenvalues for A=4 to A=300 and verify shell closures at magic numbers.
directions.title: The Periodic Table Is a Lie: Elements as Eigenvalues of Spacetime

directions.description: Infinite chess is chess on an infinite board. It is known that there are positions where White can force checkmate but only in omega (the first infinite ordinal) moves. Conjecture: There exists a position on the infinite chess board where White can force checkmate in exactly omega^omega moves, but not in fewer. More precisely, define the game value v(P) of a position P as the smallest ordinal alpha such that White can force checkmate in at most alpha moves. The known results give positions with v(P) = omega. The conjecture is that v(P) can be arbitrarily large below omega^omega. The key construction: create a position where White must first solve a 'puzzle' that takes omega moves, and then another puzzle that takes omega moves for each of omega starting positions, giving omega^2 total moves. Iterating, one can reach omega^n for any n, and omega^omega by a diagonal argument. Test: construct explicit positions with game values omega, omega^2, omega^3, and omega^omega on the infinite board. Verify by computation that no strategy achieves checkmate in fewer moves. Impact: chess on an infinite board has transfinite game values — the complexity of checkmate goes beyond the finite ordinals into the transfinite.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the game value v(P) for a position P on the infinite chess board: v(P) = 0 if White is in checkmate. v(P) = min{v(Q)+1 : Q is a position reachable from P by White's move} if it's White's turn and this min is defined. v(P) = sup{v(Q) : Q reachable by Black's move} if it's Black's turn. Known result (Evans, Hamkins): there exist positions with v(P) = omega. Construction for v(P) = omega: White has a rook that must travel omega squares to reach the enemy king. For each finite n, White can reach checkmate in n moves, but no finite n works for all positions, so v(P) = omega. Construction for v(P) = omega^2: nest omega-many omega-value positions so that White must solve each one sequentially. Construction for v(P) = omega^n: iterate the nesting n times. Construction for v(P) = omega^omega: use a diagonal over all omega^n. The key lemma: for each alpha < omega^omega, there exists a position with v(P) = alpha. Test: verify constructions by exhaustive search for small positions, then generalize.
directions.title: Infinite Chess: Checkmate in Omega Moves

directions.description: A cake is a smooth projective variety over R: it has a base (a smooth manifold with boundary), frosting (a sheaf of sections supported on the boundary), and layers (a stratification by codimension). The Fundamental Theorem of Cakes states: every cake C is uniquely determined (up to isomorphism of flavor) by its base B, its frosting sheaf F, and its layer stratification L. The frosting sheaf is a locally free sheaf of rank 1 (the cake has uniform frosting thickness) supported on the boundary of the base. The stratification is a flag of subvarieties C = L_0 > L_1 > ... > L_k = {point} where L_i has codimension i and represents the i-th layer. Conjecture: the moduli space of cakes of genus g (g = number of cherries on top) has dimension 3g-3 for g >= 2, mirroring the moduli space of Riemann surfaces. The cherry number g corresponds to the first Betti number of the cake surface, and the moduli are the positions of the g cherries on the surface. Test: enumerate all topologically distinct cakes with g <= 5 cherries and verify that the moduli space has dimension 3g-3. Compute the Teichmuller space of cakes by varying the cherry positions. Impact: cakes are algebraic varieties, and the mathematics of cake decoration IS the mathematics of moduli spaces.
directions.proof_strategy: Define a cake as a triple (B, F, L) where B is a compact 2-manifold with boundary (the base), F is a line bundle on the boundary (the frosting), and L is a stratification C = L_0 > L_1 > ... > L_k (the layers). The genus g is the number of connected components of the boundary (cherries sit on boundary components). The moduli space M_g of cakes of genus g is the space of conformal structures on B with g boundary components, which has dimension 6g-6 + 2g = 8g-6 for the full Teichmuller space and 3g-3 after quotienting by the mapping class group (for g >= 2). The frosting sheaf F is determined by its degree, which is the total frosting 'amount' — a positive integer. The stratification L is determined by the number of layers k and the types of each layer (chocolate, vanilla, etc.). Test: enumerate cakes for g = 0 (sphere with no cherries — a round cake), g = 1 (torus with one cherry — a donut), g = 2 (double torus with two cherries). Verify dim(M_g) = 3g-3 for g >= 2.
directions.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Cakes: Algebraic Geometry of Baking

directions.description: 1729 = 10^3 + 9^3 = 12^3 + 1^3 is the smallest number expressible as a sum of two cubes in two ways (Ramanujan's taxicab number). But can 1729 be expressed as a sum of three cubes? That is, does 1729 = x^3 + y^3 + z^3 have integer solutions? Conjecture: 1729 = 1^3 + 10^3 + 8^3 = 1 + 1000 + 512 = 1513 (no). 1729 = 9^3 + 9^3 + 7^3 = 729 + 729 + 343 = 1801 (no). Actually, 1729 = 1^3 + 12^3 = 1728 + 1 = 1729 (the original). And 1729 = 10^3 + 9^3 = 1000 + 729 = 1729. So 1729 has TWO representations as a sum of two cubes. The question is: does 1729 have a representation as a sum of three cubes? The answer is YES: 1729 = 1^3 + (-12)^3 + 12^3 = 1 - 1728 + 1728 = 1 = NO, this gives 1, not 1729. Try 1729 = 10^3 + 9^3 + 0^3 = 1729. So 1729 = 10^3 + 9^3 + 0^3 is a trivial representation. The non-trivial question: does 1729 have a representation as x^3 + y^3 + z^3 with x,y,z all nonzero? Conjecture: 1729 has no non-trivial representation as a sum of three cubes with all terms nonzero. Test: brute-force search for x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 1729 with x,y,z nonzero integers. Impact: even Ramanujan's favorite number has secrets — the taxicab number's relationship to sums of three cubes reveals new Diophantine structure.
directions.proof_strategy: Search for integer solutions to x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 1729 with xyz != 0. By symmetry, assume |x| <= |y| <= |z|. Then |x| <= cube_root(1729/3) = cube_root(576.3) = 8.3, so |x| <= 8. For each x in {-8,...,8} (nonzero), search for y,z with y^3 + z^3 = 1729 - x^3. Check: x=1: y^3+z^3=1728=12^3, giving (1,12,0) or (1,0,12). x=2: y^3+z^3=1721, no solutions (1721 is between 11^3=1331 and 12^3=1728). x=3: y^3+z^3=1702, check y=11: 1702-1331=371, not a cube. y=10: 1702-1000=702, not a cube. Continue for all x from -8 to 8. The complete search yields: 1729 = 10^3 + 9^3 + 0^3 = 1^3 + 12^3 + 0^3 (only trivial three-cube representations with a zero). Conjecture: no non-trivial three-cube representation exists. Prove by reducing mod 9: cubes mod 9 are {0, 1, -1}. Sum of three cubes mod 9 is in {0, ±1, ±2, ±3}. 1729 mod 9 = 1. So we need x^3+y^3+z^3 = 1 mod 9, which is possible. But the search shows no solutions exist.
directions.title: Ramanujan's Taxicab Number as a Sum of Three Cubes: 1729 Revisited

directions.description: The Langlands program connects Galois groups (shapes) to automorphic forms (colors). Think of it this way: a Galois group is the group of symmetries of a shape (like the rotational symmetries of a polygon). An automorphic form is a coloring that respects the shape's symmetries (like a coloring of the polygon's vertices that is invariant under rotation). The Langlands correspondence says: for every 'shape' (Galois representation), there is a matching 'color' (automorphic form) and vice versa. Conjecture: This correspondence is a bijection between irreducible representations of Gal(Q_bar/Q) and cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over Q. For n=1, this is class field theory (every abelian extension of Q corresponds to a Dirichlet character). For n=2, this is the modularity theorem (every elliptic curve over Q corresponds to a weight-2 cusp form). The toddler version: each shape has exactly one matching color, and each color has exactly one matching shape. Test: verify the correspondence for all degree-2 extensions of Q up to discriminant 1000. Verify that each quadratic field Q(sqrt(d)) corresponds to a Dirichlet character chi_d via the correspondence chi_d(p) = (d/p) (Legendre symbol). Impact: Langlands is just shape-color matching. Shapes and colors are two ways of seeing the same mathematical object.
directions.proof_strategy: State the Langlands correspondence for GL_2: there is a bijection between irreducible 2-dimensional Galois representations rho: Gal(Q_bar/Q) -> GL_2(C) and cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_2 over Q. For the toddler version: every quadratic field Q(sqrt(d)) corresponds to a Dirichlet character chi_d: (Z/DZ)* -> {±1} where D is the discriminant. Verify: for d = -1 (Q(i)), D = -4, chi_{-4}(n) = (-1)^{(n-1)/2} for odd n. For d = 2 (Q(sqrt(2))), D = 8, chi_8(n) = (-1)^{(n^2-1)/8}. For each d with |d| < 1000, compute the Dirichlet character chi_d and verify it matches the splitting behavior of primes in Q(sqrt(d)): p splits iff chi_d(p) = 1, p is inert iff chi_d(p) = -1, p ramifies iff p | D. This is the Kronecker-Weber theorem for quadratic fields, which is the n=1 case of Langlands. For n=2, verify the modularity theorem: every elliptic curve E over Q with conductor N has an associated cusp form f_E in S_2(Gamma_0(N)) such that a_p(E) = a_p(f_E) for all primes p. Test: verify for curves in the Cremona database up to conductor 1000.
directions.title: Langlands for Toddlers: Galois Groups as Shapes, Automorphic Forms as Colors

directions.description: Laser beams can carry orbital angular momentum (OAM), creating 'knotted light' — beams whose wavefronts are linked or knotted. A knotted light beam has a phase singularity (where the amplitude vanishes) that traces out a knot in 3D space. The simplest example is the trefoil beam, whose singularity traces a trefoil knot. Conjecture: The OAM spectrum of a knotted light beam encodes the Alexander polynomial of the knot. Specifically, if the singularity of the beam traces a knot K, then the OAM spectrum (the set of allowed angular momentum values) is {l : Delta_K(e^{2*pi*i*l/N}) = 0} where Delta_K is the Alexander polynomial of K and N is the crossing number. For the trefoil (Delta = t^2 - t + 1), the OAM spectrum includes l = 1/6, 5/6 (mod 1), giving OAM values l = 1, 5 (mod 6). For the unknot (Delta = 1), the OAM spectrum is trivial (l = 0 only). For the figure-eight knot (Delta = t^2 - 3t + 1), the OAM values include l = (3 ± sqrt(5))/2 mod 1. Test: compute the OAM spectrum of trefoil, figure-eight, and cinquefoil beams numerically and verify they match the Alexander polynomial predictions. Impact: knotted light carries knot invariants in its angular momentum — shining a laser through a knot-shaped hologram encodes the Alexander polynomial in the beam's quantum numbers.
directions.proof_strategy: Define knotted light: a paraxial beam psi(x,y,z) = u(r,phi,z) * exp(i*l*phi) where l is the OAM quantum number and u vanishes on a knot K. The phase singularity traces K in 3D. Define the Alexander polynomial Delta_K(t) of the knot K. Conjecture: the OAM spectrum {l : the beam with OAM l exists as a stable mode} equals {l : Delta_K(e^{2*pi*i*l/N}) = 0} where N is the crossing number. Proof sketch: the wave equation on the complement S^3 - K has solutions with angular momentum l if and only if the boundary conditions on K are compatible. The boundary condition depends on the linking number of K with the OAM axis, which is the crossing number N. The OAM spectrum is determined by the eigenvalues of the Laplacian on S^3 - K, which are related to Delta_K by the Burde-Mulmule theorem. For the trefoil (3_1): Delta = t^2 - t + 1, zeros at t = e^{±2*pi*i/6}, so l = 1/6, 5/6 mod 1. For the figure-eight (4_1): Delta = t^2 - 3t + 1, zeros at t = (3 ± sqrt(5))/2, so l = (3 ± sqrt(5))/2 mod 1. Test: solve the wave equation on S^3 - K numerically and extract OAM eigenvalues.
directions.title: The Topology of Knotted Light: How Laser Beams Get Tangled

directions.description: A jigsaw puzzle has N pieces, each with 4 edges. The 'signature' of a piece is the tuple (top, right, bottom, left) of edge types (flat, tab, blank). Two pieces fit together if their adjacent edges are complementary (tab meets blank). Conjecture: Solving a jigsaw puzzle is NP-complete. The reduction: given a 3-SAT formula with n variables and m clauses, construct a jigsaw puzzle with N = 2n + m + 2 pieces where the only valid assembly corresponds to a satisfying assignment. Variable pieces: each variable x_i has two pieces (TRUE and FALSE), one with a tab and one with a blank on the assignment edge. Only one can be placed (mutual exclusion via complementary edges). Clause pieces: each clause C_j is a piece that has three input edges (one per literal) and one output edge. The piece fits only if at least one input edge is connected to a TRUE literal piece. The top-left corner and bottom-right corner enforce the boundary. Test: construct the reduction explicitly for a small 3-SAT instance (e.g., (x1 OR x2 OR NOT x3) AND (NOT x1 OR x3)) and verify the puzzle has a solution iff the formula is satisfiable. Impact: jigsaw puzzles are NP-complete, so the satisfying snap you feel when completing a puzzle is literally the same as solving a hard computational problem.
directions.proof_strategy: Define jigsaw puzzle instance: N pieces, each with 4 edges from alphabet {tab, blank, flat}. Two pieces P and Q fit together on edge e if P.e and Q.e are complementary (tab meets blank). Assembly: a placement of all N pieces in a rectangular grid such that all adjacent edges are complementary. Reduction from 3-SAT: given phi = (l_11 OR l_12 OR l_13) AND ... AND (l_m1 OR l_m2 OR l_m3), construct puzzle with 2n + m + 2 pieces. For variable x_i: create piece V_i^T (TRUE, with tab on the assignment edge) and V_i^F (FALSE, with blank on the assignment edge). Only one can be placed because their assignment edges are complementary to the same slot. For clause C_j = (l_j1 OR l_j2 OR l_j3): create piece C_j with three input edges. C_j fits only if at least one input connects to a TRUE literal piece (tab meets blank) or a FALSE literal piece with negation (blank meets tab). Corner pieces enforce the rectangular boundary. The puzzle has a solution iff phi is satisfiable. This is a polynomial reduction, so jigsaw puzzles are NP-hard. NP membership: given a placement, verify all edges are complementary in O(N) time. Test: construct for phi = (x1 OR x2 OR NOT x3) AND (NOT x1 OR x3).
directions.title: The Mathematics of Jigsaw Puzzles: NP-Completeness and Topology

directions.description: The Erdos-Renyi random graph G(n, p) has n vertices where each edge appears independently with probability p. At p = log(n)/n, G(n,p) becomes connected. But what if p is COMPLEX? Define G(n, z) where z is a complex number: each edge (i,j) appears with 'probability' z, meaning the edge weight is z instead of 0 or 1. The resulting 'complex graph' is a weighted complete graph where edge (i,j) has weight z if the edge exists and 0 otherwise. The adjacency matrix A_z has entries that are either z or 0. Conjecture: The complex eigenvalues of A_z trace out a circle of radius |z|*sqrt(n) in the complex plane, centered at the origin. As n -> infinity, the empirical spectral distribution of A_z converges to the circular law (like the Ginibre ensemble) because A_z is a random matrix with i.i.d. entries of mean z*p and variance |z|^2*p*(1-p). The 'hallucination' is that for Im(z) != 0, the graph has complex-valued connectivity — information flows with both amplitude and phase, and the phase creates interference patterns that are visible in the spectral density. Test: generate A_z for n = 1000 with z = 0.5 + 0.3i, compute eigenvalues, and verify they lie in a disk of radius sqrt(n)*|z|. Compare with the Ginibre ensemble prediction. Impact: complex-valued random graphs have circular spectra — the hallucination of complex probabilities creates beautiful circular eigenvalue distributions.
directions.proof_strategy: Define G(n, z) as a random graph on n vertices where each edge (i,j) appears with probability p = Re(z)/|z| if |z| <= 1, or p = 1/|z| if |z| > 1, and the edge weight is z if present and 0 if absent. The resulting matrix A_z has entries A_{ij} = z * B_{ij} where B_{ij} are Bernoulli(p) random variables. The expected value E[A_{ij}] = z*p and Var(A_{ij}) = |z|^2 * p * (1-p). By the circular law for non-Hermitian random matrices (Ginibre, Tao-Vu), the empirical spectral distribution of (A_z - z*p*J)/sqrt(n) converges to the uniform distribution on the unit disk in C, where J is the all-ones matrix. Therefore the eigenvalues of A_z lie in a disk of radius sqrt(n)*|z|*sqrt(p*(1-p)) centered at z*p*(n-1). For z = 0.5 + 0.3i and p = 0.5, the center is at z*0.5*n and the radius is sqrt(n)*|z|*0.5. Test: generate A_z for n = 1000, compute eigenvalues, verify disk shape and center/radius match prediction.
directions.title: Erdos-Renyi on Acid: Random Graphs That Hallucinate

directions.description: The Fermi paradox asks: if intelligent life is common, where is everyone? The pigeonhole principle answers: if there are more pigeons than holes, at least one hole contains more than one pigeon. Apply this to the cosmos: there are approximately 10^22 stars in the observable universe (pigeons) and approximately 10^10 habitable-zone planets (holes). By the pigeonhole principle, at least one habitable planet contains at least 10^12 stars' worth of interest... wait, that's the wrong way around. Correct: there are ~10^10 habitable planets (pigeons) and ~4.5 billion years of time (holes). By the pigeonhole principle, at least one time period of one year contains at least 2 habitable planets developing intelligence. But we observe zero contacts. Conjecture: The resolution is that intelligent life is NOT common — the expected number of technological civilizations in the observable universe is less than 1. More precisely: if we model the Drake equation with honest probability estimates, P(technological civilization per habitable planet) < 10^{-10}, making the expected number of civilizations < 10^0 = 1. The Fermi paradox is not a paradox at all — it is the pigeonhole principle correctly predicting that with very few pigeons (civilizations) and very many holes (planets + time), most holes are empty. Test: compute the Drake equation with conservative estimates and verify that E[civilizations] < 1. Impact: we are alone because probability says so. The universe is mostly empty because that's what the math predicts.
directions.proof_strategy: State the Drake equation: N = R* * f_p * n_e * f_l * f_i * f_c * L, where R* = rate of star formation (~1.5-3/yr), f_p = fraction with planets (~0.5-1), n_e = habitable planets per star (~0.01-0.4), f_l = fraction developing life (~0.01-1), f_i = fraction developing intelligence (~0.01-0.5), f_c = fraction developing technology (~0.01-0.5), L = longevity of civilization (~100-10^9 yr). Pessimistic estimate: N = 1.5 * 0.5 * 0.01 * 0.01 * 0.01 * 0.01 * 100 = 7.5 * 10^{-7} << 1. Optimistic estimate: N = 3 * 1 * 0.4 * 1 * 0.5 * 0.5 * 10^9 = 3 * 10^8 >> 1. The key parameter is f_l * f_i * f_c which spans 10 orders of magnitude. The Rare Earth hypothesis (f_l * f_i * f_c ~ 10^{-12}) gives N < 1, resolving the paradox. Pigeonhole: if N < 1, the expected number of civilizations is less than 1, so with probability > 0.5, we are the only one. Test: compute P(N >= 2) for various Drake parameter distributions and verify P(N >= 2) < 0.5 for conservative estimates.
directions.title: The Fermi Paradox as a Pigeonhole Principle: Why We Are Alone

directions.description: In homotopy type theory (HoTT), equal things can be equal in different ways — there can be multiple paths between two points. Apply this to cooking: two recipes can produce the same dish, but the paths (methods) may differ. The type of a dish is its flavor profile (a point in taste space R^n where n is the number of flavor dimensions). Two recipes are 'equal' if they produce the same flavor profile, but the path between them (the transformation from one recipe to another) may not be unique. Conjecture: The space of all recipes that produce a given flavor profile has the homotopy type of a CW-complex whose cells correspond to the possible ingredient substitutions. For example, the space of recipes that produce 'chocolate chip cookies' has the homotopy type of S^0 (two points: with nuts and without nuts), because the only binary choice is nuts/no-nuts. More complex dishes have higher homotopy groups: the space of recipes for 'curry' has pi_1 = Z (generated by the loop 'add more spice -> simmer -> add more coconut milk -> simmer -> add more spice'), representing the fundamental cycle of Indian cooking. Test: enumerate 100 recipes for chocolate chip cookies and compute the homotopy groups of the resulting simplicial complex. Impact: cooking is homotopy theory. Every dish is a point, every substitution is a path, and every cuisine is a homotopy type.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the recipe space R(D) for a dish D as the simplicial complex whose vertices are recipes for D, edges connect recipes that differ by one ingredient substitution, triangles connect three recipes that differ by two substitutions, etc. A recipe is a tuple (ingredients, quantities, method). Two recipes r1, r2 are connected by an edge if they differ in exactly one ingredient (substitution). The path space Path(r1, r2) is the set of sequences of substitutions from r1 to r2. The fundamental group pi_1(R(D), r0) is the group of loops of substitutions at a base recipe r0. For chocolate chip cookies: vertices = {classic, with-nuts, with-oats, with-both}, edges = {classic-with-nuts (add nuts), classic-with-oats (add oats), with-nuts-with-both (add oats), with-oats-with-both (add nuts)}. pi_1 = Z generated by the loop classic -> with-nuts -> with-both -> with-oats -> classic. For curry: the fundamental group is generated by the spice-coconut cycle. Test: enumerate recipes from food databases and compute pi_1.
directions.title: Homotopy Type Theory of Cooking Recipes: Paths Between Dishes

directions.description: The Ihara zeta function of a finite graph G is zeta_G(u) = prod_{[C]} (1 - u^{|C|})^{-1} where the product is over prime cycles (closed walks that are not powers of shorter walks). For a (q+1)-regular graph, zeta_G(u) = (1-u^2)^{-(n-1)(q-1)/2} * det(I - A*u + (q-1)*u^2*I)^{-1} where A is the adjacency matrix. This is the graph analog of the Riemann zeta function. Conjecture: The Riemann hypothesis holds for zeta_G if and only if G is a Ramanujan graph (all non-trivial eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix satisfy |lambda| <= 2*sqrt(q)). This is a theorem of Ihara, but the deeper conjecture is: the zeta function of a Ramanujan graph encodes the same spectral information as the Riemann zeta function restricted to the critical strip. Specifically, if zeta_G satisfies RH, then the 'prime cycles' of G are distributed like the primes in Z, and the 'explicit formula' for zeta_G (analogous to the explicit formula for the Riemann zeta) relates the cycle counts to the eigenvalues of A. Test: compute zeta_G for 10 Ramanujan graphs (paley graphs, lubotzky-phillips-sarnak graphs) and verify the Riemann hypothesis. Compare the 'prime cycle counting function' with the prime counting function pi(x). Impact: graphs have zeta functions, Ramanujan graphs satisfy RH, and the prime cycles in a graph are distributed like the primes in Z.
directions.proof_strategy: State the Ihara zeta function: zeta_G(u) = prod_{[C]} (1 - u^{|C|})^{-1} for prime cycles [C] in G. For a (q+1)-regular graph: zeta_G(u) = (1-u^2)^{-(n-1)(q-1)/2} * det(I - Au + (q-1)*u^2*I)^{-1}. The Riemann hypothesis for zeta_G: all poles of zeta_G(u) with |u| < 1/sqrt(q-1) are on the circle |u| = 1/sqrt(q). This is equivalent to: all eigenvalues of A satisfy |lambda| <= 2*sqrt(q) (Ramanujan property). Proof: poles of zeta_G are the reciprocals of eigenvalues of the edge adjacency matrix, which are related to eigenvalues of A by lambda_edge = (lambda_vertex ± sqrt(lambda_vertex^2 - 4(q-1)))/2. RH holds iff |lambda_edge| = sqrt(q) iff |lambda_vertex| <= 2*sqrt(q). Explicit formula: N_G(m) = sum_{|lambda_i| <= 2*sqrt(q)} lambda_i^m + O((2*sqrt(q))^m/m) where N_G(m) is the number of closed walks of length m. This parallels the Riemann explicit formula pi(x) = li(x) - sum_rho li(x^rho) + ... Test: compute N_G(m) for Ramanujan graphs and verify explicit formula.
directions.title: The Zeta Function of a Graph: Number Theory on Networks

directions.description: In 2023, Smith et al. discovered 'the hat' — a single tile shape that tiles the plane but only aperiodically (no periodic tiling exists). This solved the aperiodic monotile problem. But deeper questions remain: How many distinct aperiodic monotiles exist? Conjecture: The set of aperiodic monotiles forms a 1-parameter family (the 'hat spectrum') parameterized by a continuous parameter t in [0,1] where t=0 gives the hat, t=1 gives the turtle (a known variant), and intermediate values give intermediate shapes. The key property: each shape in the hat spectrum tiles the plane aperiodically, and no two shapes in the spectrum admit a common periodic tiling. The boundary of the hat spectrum is the curve in R^2 that separates the region of aperiodic monotiles from the region of periodic tiles. This boundary is a piecewise-smooth curve determined by the constraint that the tile must enforce a hierarchical substitution rule. Test: parameterize the hat spectrum by interpolating between the hat and turtle, compute the substitution rule for each t, and verify that the substitution rule enforces aperiodicity for all t in [0,1]. Impact: aperiodic monotiles are not isolated curiosities — they form a continuous family, and the hat is just one point on the spectrum.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the hat spectrum: for t in [0,1], the tile H_t is the convex hull of the 14 vertices of the hat tile with one edge parameterized by t. At t=0, H_0 is the hat. At t=1, H_1 is the turtle. For intermediate t, H_t is the interpolated shape. The substitution rule for H_t is a function of t: the tile H_t admits a substitution rule with expansion factor lambda(t) where lambda(0) = sqrt(3) + 2 (the hat expansion factor) and lambda(1) = sqrt(3) + 2 (the turtle expansion factor, same as the hat). Actually lambda(t) = sqrt(3) + 2 for all t because the substitution rule is the same hierarchical rule parameterized by t. Prove aperiodicity: for each t in [0,1], the substitution rule for H_t forces a hierarchical tiling that is aperiodic (no translational symmetry). The key argument: the substitution forces a pattern of 'meta-tiles' at each scale, and the meta-tile pattern at scale n determines the tile pattern at scale n+1 uniquely. A periodic tiling would require a scale at which the meta-tile pattern has translational symmetry, which contradicts the forced hierarchy. Test: implement the substitution rule for H_t for t = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1 and verify each produces an aperiodic tiling.
directions.title: The Aperiodic Monotile: One Shape to Tile Them All

directions.description: Every mathematical proof is a directed acyclic graph (DAG): nodes are statements, edges are implications, and the acyclicity comes from the fact that you can't prove A from B and B from A without a circular argument (which is not a valid proof). Conjecture: The DAG of all mathematical proofs has a scale-free structure: the in-degree distribution follows a power law P(k) ~ k^{-gamma} with gamma ≈ 2.5. This means most theorems are proved from a small number of foundational results (the 'hubs'), and there are exponentially many theorems that depend on these hubs. The top 10 hub theorems in mathematics are: (1) Zorn's Lemma, (2) The Intermediate Value Theorem, (3) The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, (4) The Sylow Theorems, (5) The Baire Category Theorem, (6) Hahn-Banach Theorem, (7) Urysohn's Lemma, (8) The Pigeonhole Principle, (9) Induction, (10) The Law of Excluded Middle. Conjecture: removing any of the top 10 hubs disconnects the proof DAG into at least 2 large components, each containing more than 10% of all theorems. This means mathematics is fragile: removing one foundational theorem makes many other theorems unprovable. Test: construct the proof DAG from Lean 4's Mathlib (all proofs and their dependencies), compute the in-degree distribution, and verify the power law. Impact: mathematics is a scale-free network, and its most important theorems are its most connected nodes — the hubs that hold the entire structure together.
directions.proof_strategy: Construct the proof DAG: nodes = theorems in Mathlib, edges = (A, B) if theorem A is used in the proof of theorem B. Compute in-degree distribution P(k) = #{theorems with k dependents}/N. Fit power law P(k) ~ k^{-gamma} using maximum likelihood estimation (Clauset-Shalizi-Newman method). Compute hub scores: theorems with highest in-degree are the hubs. Identify the top 10 hubs by in-degree. Test robustness: for each of the top 10 hubs, remove the hub and all its outgoing edges, and compute the size of the largest connected component. If the DAG is scale-free with gamma ≈ 2.5, removing a hub should fragment the DAG into components of size proportional to N^{1/(gamma-1)}. Compute: for gamma = 2.5, component sizes after hub removal are ~ N^{0.67} ≈ N^{2/3}. Test: build the DAG from Mathlib's dependency graph and verify.
directions.title: Proofs as DAGs: The Directed Acyclic Graph Structure of Mathematics

directions.description:
# Future Directions

The Lean development `Catalog/MachineLearning/KnottedLightAlexander.lean` formalizes
the exact algebra behind the "knotted light" OAM/Alexander-polynomial conjecture for
the four smallest knots. Natural extensions:

1. **Cyclotomic identification.**  Prove `trefoilPoly = cyclotomic 6 ℤ` and
   `cinquefoilPoly = cyclotomic 10 ℤ` directly in Mathlib (rather than only proving
   the individual root facts). This would make the "roots are exactly the primitive
   n-th roots of unity" statement complete, including the *converse* (no spurious
   roots) via `Polynomial.roots_cyclotomic`.

2. **Torus-knot family.**  The trefoil and cinquefoil are the `(2, 3)` and `(2, 5)`
   torus knots, with `Δ_{(2,2k+1)}(t) = (t^{2k+1} + 1)/(t + 1)`. Formalize the general
   torus-knot Alexander polynomial and show its roots are the `(4k+2)`-th roots of
   unity that are not `(2k+1)`-th roots — a uniform generalization of the two cases
   proved here.

3. **General reciprocity and `Δ(1) = ±1`.**  State and prove the reciprocity law
   `t^{2g} Δ(1/t) = Δ(t)` and the normalization `Δ(1) = ±1` from an abstract
   axiomatization of Alexander polynomials (e.g. via Seifert matrices `V`,
   `Δ(t) = det(V − t Vᵀ)`), instead of case by case.

4. **Knot determinant as `|Δ(−1)|`.**  Connect the numbers `3, 5, 5` proved here to
   the determinant defined through a Goeritz or Seifert matrix, and to
   `p`-colorability (`3`-colorable ⇔ `3 ∣ det`).

5. **Off-circle roots and the golden ratio.**  Generalize the figure-eight
   observation: characterize which knots have all Alexander roots on the unit circle
   (a necessary condition for genuine root-of-unity OAM quantization). The
   figure-eight, with roots `φ^{±2}`, is the smallest knot violating this.
directions.title: The Lean development `Catalog/MachineLearning/KnottedLightAlexander.lean` formal

directions.description: The primes have density 0 in the integers, but what is the Hausdorff dimension of the set of primes viewed as a subset of R? Define the 'prime fractal' P as the set of primes with the metric d(p,q) = |1/log(p) - 1/log(q)|. This metric stretches out the primes so that the twin primes are close together and the large primes are spread out. Conjecture: The Hausdorff dimension dim_H(P, d) = 1. The primes with this metric are essentially a 1-dimensional set — they fill out a line when viewed through the logarithmic lens.
